## Review baseline and contract

- Baseline commit: `e068580e0f492b32e737ed202285759a388e7697`
- Branch state at start: clean and synchronized with `origin/quantum-computing-book`
- Scope: every tracked file under `book/**` at the baseline commit: 67 files total (48 Markdown files and 19 SVG files)
- Exclusions: everything outside `book/**`; existing material in `reviews/**` is historical input and is not part of the review corpus. This ledger is an output artifact only.
- Independence: each book unit will be reviewed on its present text and merits without consulting earlier review ledgers during the section-level pass.
- Reading discipline: only one book file will be open for review at a time. Markdown will be read in small semantic units, and findings will be appended here immediately after each unit. SVGs will likewise be handled one file at a time, with both source-structure and rendered-visual inspection.
- Review dimensions: correctness; stated and unstated assumptions; domains and qualifications; notation and internal consistency; pedagogy; cognitive load and pacing; accessibility; links, figures, and cross-references; defects; probable concerns; slight suspicions and unresolved doubts; optional refinements; concrete improvement ideas; positive notes; and reader entertainment/engagement.
- Completion gates: full file and unit coverage reconciliation; structural and visual SVG coverage; cross-book consistency audits; prioritized remediation; and a final synthesis.
- Process constraints: no sub-agents; no commits unless explicitly requested.

## Fine-grained review

### `book/00-front-matter/00-preface.md`

#### Title, production-status banner, and navigation (lines 1–5)

- **Positive note — orientation:** The plain `Preface` title and immediately available table-of-contents/next-page links make the entry point mechanically clear. The directional arrow on the next link is useful visual affordance, and the explicit destination title reduces click uncertainty.
- **Probable concern — production metadata on the reading surface:** `Status: prereviewed`, `Phase: 6`, and `Sections drafted: 12 / 12` read as internal workflow state rather than durable book content. `prereviewed` is also easy to parse as “not yet reviewed,” which may reduce confidence before the argument begins. If this is the public reading surface, remove the banner or translate it into stable edition metadata; if it is intentionally a living-draft signal, define the status vocabulary once and automate it so it cannot silently become stale.
- **Slight suspicion — navigation semantics:** `Recommended / Assumed Background and Self-Check` is informative but long, and the slash can mean either an alternative or a compound label. A shorter link label such as `Next: Background and self-check` would scan more smoothly while the destination page supplies the fuller nuance.
- **Consistency check for later:** Verify across all Markdown files that status banners use the same vocabulary and that previous/next links match actual reading order, capitalization, and filenames. The current banner’s `12 / 12` should also be reconciled with the actual number of level-two sections: the heading map shows twelve only if every post-title section is counted consistently.
- **Accessibility:** Link meaning does not depend on the arrow alone, which is good. The middle-dot separators are compact but may be read aloud; this is a minor issue, not a blocker.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** Neutral. The opening is functional rather than inviting; the workflow banner delays the book’s voice by one visual beat. Beginning directly with the purpose statement would create a cleaner first impression.

#### “Why This Book Exists” — polarized reputations and the proposed middle (lines 9–18)

- **Positive note — hook and voice:** The opposing caricatures form a brisk, intelligible hook, and the pivot from hype-versus-dismissal to “young engineering discipline” gives the book a confident reason to exist. The escalating list culminating in curing disease is lively without becoming jokey. Entertainment is **high for expository front matter**: it creates tension, then promises resolution.
- **Probable concern — breadth of the dismissal/hype framing:** “To one camp” and “to another” are explicitly rhetorical categories, but `two reputations` may still imply an exhaustive public taxonomy. A small qualifier—“two prominent reputations”—would preserve the energy while acknowledging informed positions between them.
- **Probable concern — time-sensitive strength:** “a software stack that is converging fast enough” is a broad, contestable 2026 claim. Toolchains share concepts but remain fragmented across providers, intermediate representations, error-mitigation stacks, and rapidly changing APIs. Either specify what is converging (circuit abstractions, common workflow stages, interoperability standards) or soften to “maturing fast enough.” This should be checked against the later tooling chapter.
- **Qualification opportunity:** “real machines you can program today” is true in the access sense, but risks implying ordinary production usefulness. Adding “experiment with” or “access and program” would harmonize with the promise of sober limits without weakening the case for learning.
- **Style/pacing:** The first paragraph is one long rhetorical sweep, but its clauses remain controlled and the final four-part list lands well. No split is necessary; a split would likely reduce momentum.

#### “Why This Book Exists” — the desired treatment and its standards (lines 20–29)

- **Positive note — concrete editorial contract:** The four `does not` clauses clearly state the book’s pedagogical principles, while the rigor/practice contrast identifies where formalism and engineering judgment will dominate. This is unusually useful preface material because readers can later hold the book accountable to it.
- **Slight suspicion — “self-contained” overpromise:** A single book can introduce prerequisites, but later quantum information, complexity, hardware, and fault-tolerance material may still require external depth. Consider “substantially self-contained” or define the intended meaning here (all notation and prerequisites needed for the book’s core path are introduced). The background self-check may supply that definition, so cross-check before recommending a change.
- **Slight suspicion — “rigor matters” phrasing:** Rigor also matters for hardware claims and SDK guidance; the intended distinction seems to be proof-oriented foundations versus empirically contingent engineering practice. Rephrasing to “formally rigorous on…” and “engineering-grounded on…” would avoid suggesting that rigor ceases to matter outside the named subjects.
- **Consistency/coverage check for later:** The named promises—measurement, unitarity, error correction, complexity, physical gate sets, SDK workflows, and critical metric reading—should each receive explicit, discoverable treatment. Track these as preface-to-body contract items in the final audit.
- **Accessibility:** “unitarity” arrives without explanation, acceptable in a promise paragraph because the audience need not understand it yet. The parallel syntax makes a dense sentence navigable.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The first-person motivation humanizes the project, and “analogies that fall apart at the second question” is memorable. The abstract rigor/practice list cools the rhetoric slightly but increases trust.

#### “Why This Book Exists” — positioning against textbooks and popular science (lines 31–44)

- **Positive note — market positioning:** The passage names a recognizable reference point, describes its strengths respectfully, and identifies the proposed gap. This is more credible than dismissing established texts merely to elevate the new one.
- **Probable concern — false binary / unsupported survey claim:** `Most existing texts fall into one of two categories` is hard to sustain given the substantial middle literature: developer-oriented introductions, applied course texts, interactive notebooks, and mathematically serious books for non-physicists. Recast as “Two common categories…” or briefly acknowledge that the book combines emphases rarely found together. The current claim invites knowledgeable readers to produce counterexamples rather than follow the argument.
- **Probable concern — mutable era label:** Calling NISQ “the current hardware era” is both time-sensitive and conceptually disputed, especially as the book itself distinguishes early fault-tolerant development. A dated formulation—“the hardware regime widely called NISQ in the 2010s and 2020s”—would age better. Chapter 25 and the 2026 timestamp note must use compatible era language.
- **Slight suspicion — comparison fairness:** Publication date explains why Nielsen–Chuang’s original edition does not cover contemporary platforms, but the sentence could sound like a defect rather than a scope/history fact. The surrounding praise mostly controls this; mentioning the edition/year would make the comparison precise.
- **Slight suspicion — audience characterization:** “assumes a level of mathematical patience” is witty but substitutes temperament for prerequisites and may sound faintly condescending to both audiences. “Sustained mathematical preparation” or a concrete prerequisite list would be clearer.
- **Accessibility and terminology:** Expanding NISQ on first use and pointing to Chapter 25 is good. The parenthesis is long and interrupts an already complex sentence; a footnote or a shorter appositive could improve flow.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** The genre contrast is easy to follow and `metaphors instead of working understanding` is sharp, but the long Nielsen–Chuang sentence carries too many qualifications and loses some snap.

#### “Why This Book Exists” — initial portrait of the intended reader (lines 46–56)

- **Positive note — respect for reader competence:** The paragraph identifies transferable experience instead of treating developers as mathematical novices. Its final density/care balance is an appealing editorial promise.
- **Strong concern — unnecessarily narrow prerequisite:** Requiring serious use of a strongly typed language has no clear connection to learning quantum computing and excludes experienced Python, JavaScript, Lisp, or dynamically typed scientific-computing practitioners. If the body depends on type-system analogies, say that such experience helps; otherwise replace this with substantial programming experience.
- **Strong concern — linear-algebra example mismatch:** “has implemented something non-trivial that uses linear algebra” is a demanding prerequisite, yet the listed examples do not reliably entail personally implementing the linear-algebra layer. Many engineers build recommenders or neural networks through libraries without manipulating vectors or matrices directly. State the actual skill—comfort with vectors, matrices, complex numbers, and basic matrix operations—and let the self-check diagnose it.
- **Probable concern — paper-reading threshold:** Comfort opening an unfamiliar-notation research paper selects for research fluency, not merely experienced software development. This conflicts somewhat with the promise not to assume a physics/theoretical-CS background. Mark it as helpful rather than required, or explain that the book teaches this reading skill.
- **Slight suspicion — duplication:** A dedicated `Who This Book Is For` section follows immediately, and another section defines `Experienced Developer`. This paragraph may preempt and duplicate both. Consider using it as a concise thesis and moving the detailed qualifications to those sections.
- **Language/accessibility:** Singular `they` is clear. “leave nothing important on the floor” is understandable but idiomatic; “omit no essential bridge” would be more globally accessible, though less lively.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The concrete project list lets readers recognize themselves, and the emphasis on respecting their time is motivating. The cumulative prerequisites may also make qualified readers feel unnecessarily screened out.

#### “Who This Book Is For” — audience statement and mathematics checklist (lines 60–75)

- **Positive note — operational prerequisites:** The text replaces vague “mathematical maturity” with named concepts and correctly tells readers that Chapter 4 is a refresher. This enables an honest self-assessment and aligns with the next front-matter page’s purpose.
- **Probable concern — prerequisite level may be overstated:** Determinants and diagonalization are listed alongside operations that recur constantly, but quantum-computing introductions can often defer or locally teach them. If they are genuinely needed before Chapter 4, identify why; otherwise separate `essential on entry` from `helpful, and reviewed`. This matters because a checklist phrased as `should be comfortable` can unnecessarily reject capable readers.
- **Correctness/precision:** `$\mathbb{C}^{2^n}$` accurately describes pure-state vectors for an $n$-qubit register, but “Most of the book lives in” may blur state-vector space with operators, density matrices, classical descriptions, and physical systems whose Hilbert-space dimension is not restricted to qubits. It works rhetorically; a precise alternative is “Much of the circuit-model mathematics begins in…”
- **Pedagogy:** Grouping probability separately is useful. `Random variables` may be less central than distributions, conditional probability, expectation, and sampling; later usage should determine whether this list reflects actual prerequisite demand.
- **Style/accessibility:** “complex arithmetic is a daily activity, not a garnish” is vivid and reassuringly direct. The fragment list (`Addition, multiplication, modulus...`) works as a checklist, though the book should standardize whether such fragments take terminal punctuation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate to high.** Prerequisite lists are intrinsically dry, but the `active toolkit` and `not a garnish` language gives this one personality without obscuring content.

#### “Who This Book Is For” — complexity and software-tooling checklist (lines 76–83)

- **Positive note — calibrated complexity expectation:** The distinction between recognizing P/NP and having studied complexity theory is helpful and lowers the correct barrier.
- **Optional refinement — “recognize it as a thing”:** The colloquial close is friendly but semantically thin. “recognize why resource scaling matters” would state the actual learning prerequisite and better prepare readers for quantum-speedup claims.
- **Strong concern — SDK/build-system criterion:** Comfort with verbose type annotations and a build system is neither necessary nor reliably correlated with quantum-computing readiness. It repeats the earlier strongly typed-language gate and may exclude notebook-oriented scientists while privileging one software culture. Replace it with comfort learning an unfamiliar library, reading API documentation, and debugging small programs—the transferable skills later hands-on work actually needs.
- **Internal-consistency check:** Determine whether the book’s examples truly use an SDK with verbose type annotations or any build system. If the practical path is Python/notebooks, this criterion is especially misleading.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** “feels like a tool, not an obstacle” has a clean cadence, but readers outside compiled-language ecosystems may experience it as gatekeeping rather than invitation.

#### “Who This Book Is For” — explicitly unnecessary prerequisites (lines 85–92)

- **Positive note — anxiety reduction:** Naming physics, advanced calculus, and group theory directly answers the most likely reader concerns. Promising local introduction of the small group-theory requirement is good scaffolding.
- **Probable concern — pedagogical-method oversimplification:** “from the postulates rather than from the historical experiments” sets up an unnecessary opposition. A postulate-first development can still use experiments for motivation, and the historical prelude may already do so. Clarify that experimental history is context rather than a prerequisite or primary derivation route.
- **Slight suspicion — computer-science textbook generalization:** “in the spirit of how computer-science textbooks present the field” lacks a clear referent: quantum computing, quantum mechanics, or formal systems generally. Naming the axiomatic/circuit-model tradition would be clearer.
- **Qualification check:** “calculus beyond first-year level” varies significantly by country and institution. Name derivatives, integrals, and elementary differential equations—or point readers to the self-check—to make the threshold portable.
- **Correctness nuance:** Matrix exponentials can be presented algebraically without calculus, while continuous-time evolution commonly uses differential equations. “chiefly” leaves room for other uses, but later chapters should be checked against this promise.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Relief and specificity sustain attention; the method comparison is more institutional than vivid.

#### “Who This Book Is For” — promised exit capabilities (lines 94–98)

- **Positive note — outcome-based contract:** The transition from name recognition to paper reading, claim evaluation, experimentation, and maturity judgment gives the book a compelling practical destination. It balances theory, practice, and epistemic caution.
- **Probable concern — extremely ambitious endpoint:** “read a current quantum algorithms paper” spans papers from accessible circuit applications to research requiring advanced representation theory, numerical analysis, or field-specific knowledge. Qualify this as “approach and critically read many current papers with appropriate references” or specify the class of papers.
- **Qualification opportunity:** Running an experiment on “real hardware” depends on external provider access, queue policies, geography, accounts, and APIs that can change. The book can teach the workflow, but should not guarantee availability; “be prepared to run” or “run where access permits” is safer.
- **Consistency gate for final audit:** These four exit claims are measurable promises. Confirm that exercises or worked examples actually assess each one, especially vendor-claim evaluation and maturity classification rather than merely discussing them.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The quoted before/after states give readers a clear progression and a satisfying reason to continue.

#### “What ‘Experienced Developer’ Means Here” — positive definition (lines 102–110)

- **Positive note — experience defined by practice:** Shipping software, reading others’ code, reasoning about correctness/performance, and crossing domain boundaries are relevant habits. This is much stronger than defining experience by years employed or mastery of a particular language.
- **Probable concern — examples mix incompatible career axes:** `mid-career`, `graduate student`, and `senior engineer` denote different experience types; a graduate student may never have shipped software, while an early-career engineer may satisfy every functional criterion. Keep the capability definition and present roles only as non-exhaustive examples.
- **Slight suspicion — title mismatch:** The section says the phrase appears in the title, but the visible file title is only `Preface`; this presumably means the book title. Ensure the book title actually contains the exact phrase and is visible nearby enough that this reference does not feel orphaned in extracted formats.
- **Inclusivity/refinement:** “shipped real software” can undervalue internal tools, open-source work, research code, safety-critical prototypes, or maintained systems that are never commercially “shipped.” “Built and maintained software used beyond a toy exercise” would retain the intended bar with fewer cultural assumptions.
- **Consistency:** This capability-based definition conflicts with earlier language-specific/toolchain prerequisites. Prefer this section’s transferable-skills framing and revise those earlier gates accordingly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The sequence of recognizable professional experiences creates identification and momentum; the role list becomes slightly résumé-like.

#### “What ‘Experienced Developer’ Means Here” — non-assumptions and proof-depth policy (lines 112–121)

- **Positive note — transparent proof policy:** Stating when the book will cite versus derive is valuable expectation-setting. The criterion—standard result versus subtle/misleading treatment—is more reader-centered than a uniform proof style.
- **Probable concern — “builds the postulates from scratch”:** Postulates are stipulated foundations, not normally built or derived. The intended claim is likely that they are introduced and motivated from scratch. This wording is conceptually important in a book that later discusses foundations; revise to “introduces the postulates from first principles” or “develops the formalism from explicitly stated postulates.”
- **Slight suspicion — “self-contained on the physics side”:** The qualifier is more defensible than globally `self-contained`, but physical intuition, hardware operation, and open-system dynamics may rely on unstated background. Define self-contained as sufficient for following the book, not exhaustive physical education.
- **Probable concern — belief framing:** “before believing it” casts citations as a substitute for warranted understanding. Technical readers generally need to know hypotheses, scope, and implications even when a proof is omitted. “before using it” or “before proceeding” would better express selective derivation without implying appeal to authority.
- **Audit criterion:** For cited-but-unproved results, verify that the later text really supplies the claimed trio—statement, worked example, and citation—and states all material conditions. Also sample every claim that standard treatments are `misleading`; such wording needs a concrete explanation and fair characterization.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** The editorial candor builds trust, though this is policy prose rather than narrative. The contrast between standard and subtle results gives a mild sense of intellectual stakes.

#### “What This Book Is Not” — purpose and prerequisite boundary (lines 125–132)

- **Positive note — reader-respecting boundary:** Explicitly helping readers decide against the book is trustworthy. Sending underprepared readers to diagnostics and alternatives turns exclusion into useful routing.
- **Slight suspicion — “next chapter”:** The linked destination is front matter, not necessarily numbered as a chapter. `Next section` or `next page` would avoid confusing the formal chapter count and match the navigation link.
- **Consistency:** The destination title again uses a slash, and here is italicized but not linked. Making this a direct relative link would improve usability in web/PDF contexts and reduce reliance on linear navigation.
- **Qualification:** The text groups three broad prerequisites as simply new/not-new, though partial preparation is common. The promised diagnostics should distinguish isolated gaps that can be repaired from genuinely wrong starting points.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low to moderate but appropriately concise.** It performs necessary triage without dwelling on it.

#### “What This Book Is Not” — rejection of equation-free overview (lines 134–139)

- **Positive note — clear epistemic stance:** “The mathematics is the explanation” is a memorable statement of method, and the distinction between vocabulary and operational understanding strongly supports the book’s identity.
- **Probable concern — audience caricature:** Equating equation-free explanation with `dinner conversation or strategic briefings` understates sophisticated conceptual, historical, policy, and philosophical treatments. This partially repeats the earlier genre binary and may alienate readers or authors unnecessarily. Praise their distinct goals without reducing their level.
- **Qualification opportunity:** Mathematics is indispensable for the promised engineering competence, but it is not the whole explanation: physical assumptions, experimental evidence, systems constraints, and conceptual interpretation also matter. “The mathematics is an indispensable part of the explanation” is harder to misread and more consistent with the hardware/practice ambitions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The sharp antithesis is quotable and energizing, though its force comes partly from overstating the contrast.

#### “What This Book Is Not” — research-monograph boundary (lines 141–144)

- **Positive note — medium awareness:** The passage sensibly distinguishes durable instructional synthesis from the latest result and promises literature pointers for moving targets.
- **Probable concern — stability criterion needs visible implementation:** `stable enough to teach` is subjective, especially in NISQ applications and hardware roadmaps. Later sections should date claims, distinguish consensus from active dispute, and cite review/primary literature rather than merely labeling material stable.
- **Slight suspicion — “absolute latest”:** No medium reliably provides an absolute latest result, and books can be continuously updated. “fast-moving frontier” is enough; the superlative adds little.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Compact and credible, with `bleeding edge` adding familiar color.

#### “What This Book Is Not” — hardware-reference boundary (lines 146–155)

- **Positive note — excellent scope calibration:** The passage names both intended competencies and concrete non-goals. Describing Part IX as a software engineer’s view is candid and useful.
- **Probable concern — overambitious intermediate claims:** Enough material to `follow a control-systems paper` and explain why a device behaves as it does can demand substantial electromagnetism, quantum optics, RF engineering, cryogenics, and platform-specific knowledge. Narrow to “follow the high-level argument of selected control-systems papers” and “reason about important contributors to behavior,” unless Part IX truly develops the prerequisites.
- **Taxonomy/consistency:** The manuscript uses `Part IX` here but directory names use `part-09`; verify displayed part numbering and consistent Roman/Arabic style throughout generated formats.
- **Accessibility:** The examples (superconducting qubit, dilution refrigerator, ion trap) make the boundary tangible even for newcomers. `view onto` is understandable but `view of` is simpler.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** Concrete hardware objects provide texture and make scope language less bureaucratic.

#### “What This Book Is Not” — vendor neutrality (lines 157–162)

- **Positive note — durable focus:** Teaching field-level concepts while identifying convention differences is the right policy for a fast-changing tool ecosystem. Naming qubit ordering, native gates, and QFT signs makes the promise testable.
- **Strong concern — vague and mutable dependency claim:** `the most widely-used open-source SDKs` needs named packages, versions, evidence or a less comparative formulation. Popularity changes and “most widely used” is difficult to establish. The hands-on chapters should expose a tested environment/lockfile and date every API-dependent example.
- **Style:** Standard publishing style is `widely used` without a hyphen after an adverb ending in `-ly`; remove the hyphen in `widely-used`.
- **Consistency check:** Earlier text implies a verbose typed SDK/build system, while this paragraph says examples are Python with common SDKs. That makes the earlier prerequisite look even less justified.
- **Technical nuance:** QFT sign is often an algorithm/transform-definition convention rather than uniquely a vendor convention. Qubit-ordering conventions can induce apparent sign/order differences in examples, but the manuscript should describe the layers precisely.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Vendor neutrality is reassuring; the concrete convention list gives a small technical preview.

#### “How to Use This Book” — scale, linear reading, and dependency promise (lines 166–172)

- **Positive note — explicit reading strategy:** Readers are told why linear order matters—dependencies, accumulated notation, and conventions—not merely commanded to follow it.
- **Exactness check:** The claimed thirteen parts and thirty-seven chapters match the filename inventory at baseline, assuming Chapters 1–37 and Parts I–XIII. This must be rechecked against displayed headings and the table of contents after all files are reviewed.
- **Strong audit obligation:** `no chapter needs a forward reference to make sense` is an absolute and unusually valuable promise. Record every forward conceptual dependency, undefined term, future-proof deferral, and necessary later citation during this pass. A forward cross-reference for optional enrichment would not violate it; a required definition or justification would.
- **Slight suspicion — conflict with selective use:** A strictly accumulating linear dependency chain and chapters that later “stand alone” are compatible only if prerequisites are explicitly summarized/linked. Review chapter openings for local prerequisite statements.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Organizational prose is clear and purposeful; the scale (37 chapters) may feel daunting without a core-path estimate, which later reading paths may solve.

#### “How to Use This Book” — Historical Prelude placement (lines 174–179)

- **Positive note — choice architecture:** The prelude’s optional status and best-fit audience are explained precisely. This prevents history-first readers from missing it and task-focused readers from fearing a dependency.
- **Consistency gate:** The claims `self-contained`, `introduces no formalism that later chapters depend on`, and `skipped entirely` should be tested both ways: the prelude must not require later notation, and numbered chapters must not rely on its definitions or examples.
- **Slight suspicion — placement language:** In a filesystem or web table of contents, the prelude may be visibly grouped as `part-00` rather than literally sitting between front matter and Chapter 1. Generated ordering is the authoritative test.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** Calling out a narrative history offers a welcome change of texture and lets readers choose their preferred entry style.

#### “How to Use This Book” — selective/reference use and appendices (lines 181–186)

- **Positive note — dual-use design:** The passage distinguishes first-pass learning from later lookup and names exactly which appendices are reference tables. This is practical information readers can act on.
- **Probable concern — “prerequisite graph explicit”:** This is a strong structural claim. Cross-references alone do not necessarily form an explicit graph unless each chapter declares prerequisites systematically. Verify whether the book offers stable anchor links, reciprocal references where useful, and enough context to know why a prerequisite matters.
- **Slight suspicion — “self-contained enough”:** Appropriately qualified but undefined. A selective reader still needs a clear prerequisite header or reading-path pointer per chapter; otherwise finding `the prerequisites` requires trial and error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low to moderate, appropriately utilitarian.** Concrete appendix names keep it from feeling generic.

#### “How to Use This Book” — sanity-check exercise policy (lines 188–198)

- **Positive note — retrieval-oriented intent:** Framing exercises as rapid diagnostics and encouraging rereading when recall fails is pedagogically sound. Distinguishing calibration from practice is useful.
- **Strong concern — withholding answers:** `the act of answering matters more than the act of looking up` does not justify omitting answers; retrieval practice and feedback are complementary. Readers cannot reliably detect a plausible but wrong answer, especially in quantum mechanics where misconceptions are subtle. Provide collapsible, delayed, appendix, or linked solutions at least for all objectively checkable exercises.
- **Probable concern — buried-answer design:** Saying a non-obvious answer exists somewhere in the discussion creates search friction and may reveal only that a phrase can be found, not the reasoning. Each exercise should have a precise section pointer or a concise solution/explanation.
- **Sentence-level issue:** `textbook-with-solutions-in-the-back sense` is cumbersome, and the following sentence is long. “These are diagnostic prompts, not a conventional end-of-chapter problem set” is cleaner.
- **Consistency audit:** Count which chapters lack exercises despite `Most`, verify the two stated exceptions, and check whether every exercise is answerable solely from preceding material without ambiguity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high in intent.** Quick self-tests can make reading active, but absent feedback risks converting engagement into frustration.

#### “How to Use This Book” — integrated worked-example policy (lines 200–203)

- **Positive note — strong pedagogical principle:** Integrating examples at the moment abstraction becomes costly generally reduces cognitive load. The formulation is concise and memorable.
- **Qualification:** Some derivations genuinely establish a general result before an example, and premature examples can anchor readers to a special case. Treat this as a default design heuristic, not a universal rule; the current wording mostly reads as principle rather than absolute mandate.
- **Audit criterion:** For each dense derivation, check whether a minimal concrete case appears before or during the first conceptual bottleneck, and whether the later generalization explicitly reconnects to it.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High for editorial guidance.** `the example is the explanation` is punchy and promises a concrete reading experience.

#### “Core Topics, Deep Dives, and Frontier Topics” — three-way framing (lines 205–208)

- **Positive note — macro-level map:** Categorizing thirteen parts into three purposes reduces the apparent scale and helps readers understand why different chapters may adopt different proof depth or temporal caution.
- **Consistency concern:** The heading says `Deep Dives`, but the three labels are `Core topics`, `Engineering reality`, and `Applications and frontier`; no content class is called a deep dive. Rename the heading or the middle category so the promised taxonomy and actual taxonomy agree.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** The prospect of moving from canon through engineering to judgment creates a satisfying arc.

#### “Core Topics…” — core topics, Parts I–VI (lines 210–216)

- **Positive note — clear curricular spine:** The list concisely communicates the foundational sequence and the competence it builds.
- **Probable concern — historical stability overgeneralization:** Algorithms, quantum information pedagogy, and even preferred circuit/measurement formalisms have evolved materially. “changed least across decades” is defensible relative to hardware/frontier chapters but should be qualified as foundational results rather than whole parts.
- **Probable concern — skip prohibition:** “cannot reasonably skip” conflicts with the selective reading promise and is too broad for readers already fluent in some foundations. Say first-time readers cannot safely skip topics they have not mastered, then route knowledgeable readers through the self-check.
- **Terminology:** Calling the whole of Parts I–VI `the canon` may unintentionally elevate the book’s precise selection/order into disciplinary consensus. “covers the established core” is less grand and more exact.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** The compact progression is reassuring, though `canon` and non-skippability make the tone more prescriptive.

#### “Core Topics…” — engineering reality, Parts VII–X (lines 218–225)

- **Positive note — algorithm-to-device gap as subject:** Treating compilation, noise, control, resource limits, and hardware behavior as first-class rather than implementation footnotes is a compelling differentiator.
- **Grammar defect:** The singular category label takes a singular verb: `Engineering reality … covers`, not `cover`—and the present text correctly uses `covers`; retain this if the label changes. The nearby plural `Parts VII through X` can tempt future edits into disagreement.
- **Taxonomy suspicion:** Complexity theory is foundational theoretical computer science, not naturally `engineering reality`. Its placement may be pedagogically right because it disciplines speedup claims, but the category description should explain the inclusion or use a broader label such as `Limits and engineering reality`.
- **Time-sensitive terminology:** `NISQ era` and `hardware is no longer hypothetical` need nuanced treatment. Experimental quantum hardware predates the NISQ label by decades; what changed is cloud access, scale, programmability, and engineering relevance. Later historical/hardware chapters should not repeat an implied “paper to real hardware only now” chronology.
- **Style:** `the same algorithm on a real device` is slightly imprecise: execution requires a mapped/compiled/noisy implementation, often not the same abstract algorithm in a simple sense. That transformation is probably the point; naming it would strengthen the sentence.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** The paper-versus-device tension is concrete and promises the practical material likely to distinguish the book.

#### “Core Topics…” — applications/frontier, Parts XI–XIII (lines 227–235)

- **Grammar defect:** The compound plural subject `Applications and frontier — Parts XI through XIII — surveys` should take `survey`, unless the label is treated explicitly as a singular category (which reads unnaturally). This is a clear copyedit.
- **Probable concern — category coherence:** Adjacent models, engineering bridges, conceptual pitfalls, and endgame perspective are not all `applications and frontier`. The label risks misrepresenting Parts XII–XIII. A broader `Applications, adjacent models, and judgment` would track the actual contents.
- **Positive note — maturity goal:** Distinguishing competence from informed judgment gives the final third a meaningful role beyond cataloguing use cases. Explicitly acknowledging aging risk is excellent epistemic hygiene.
- **Audit criterion:** “appropriate humility” should appear as dates, evidence grades, counterarguments, uncertainty ranges, and separations among demonstrated, projected, and speculative value—not merely cautious adjectives.
- **Slight suspicion — “most likely to age”:** Hardware, SDK, vendor metrics, and NISQ practice in Parts IX–X may age at least as quickly as applications. The 2026 maintenance policy should encompass all empirically mutable chapters.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The promise of learning to judge claims rather than merely accumulate facts is motivating; the long list makes the category feel diffuse.

#### “Reading Linearly vs. Reading Selectively” — concrete foundation chain (lines 239–247)

#### “A Note on Conventions” — purpose and source-renderer note (lines 312–322)

In rendered output the example naturally appears as $\{0,1\}^n$, so most readers cannot see the issue being explained. Move this to contributor documentation or a source comment, and test all output targets in the build.

#### “A Note on Conventions” — qubit significance and Qiskit mapping (lines 324–341)

- **Positive note — high-value pitfall:** Endianness/order confusion causes real errors, and the paragraph goes beyond a simplistic “Qiskit reverses bits” warning by distinguishing tensor-factor mapping. Advising readers to consult version-specific documentation is appropriately cautious.
- **Precision defect:** The integer formula should state the summation bounds, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i2^{n-i}$. An unbounded $\sum_i$ is inferable but needlessly loose in the convention-defining sentence.
- **Strong technical concern — Qiskit behavior is more layered than described:** Qubit significance, statevector basis indexing, classical-bit significance, register layout, measurement mapping, and `get_counts()` display order are related but not a single convention applied uniformly. Count keys depend on classical-bit/register ordering and explicit measurement wiring; multi-register strings can include spaces. The current `applied consistently … across … count strings` formulation risks teaching exactly the oversimplification the paragraph tries to prevent. Separate these layers and show one explicit two-qubit circuit-to-statevector-to-measurement example.
- **Probable concern — “textbook convention”:** Textbooks vary in tensor ordering and wire/layout conventions. Call it `the convention adopted in this book and many texts`, not uniquely the textbook convention.
- **Probable concern — “recommended mapping” surprise:** Mapping the leftmost factor to Qiskit’s highest-numbered qubit makes printed strings coincide, but readers need to know how this generalizes to selected/noncontiguous qubits and classical registers. Ensure §4.8 states the mapping as an explicit function and tests measurement cases.
- **Copy/pacing:** The paragraph is 18 source lines and carries at least five concepts. Split after the book’s convention, then isolate Qiskit translation in a warning/example box. The current density is especially high before readers have formally learned qubits.
- **Cross-reference:** `§4.8` must be a stable link rather than a bare typographic reference in digital output.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate for experienced Qiskit users, low for newcomers.** The puzzle is practically important, but the detail arrives before enough conceptual scaffolding and may create anxiety.

#### “A Note on Conventions” — two-qubit basis and CNOT matrix (lines 343–351)

- **Positive note — executable disambiguation:** Giving the ordered basis, control/target assignment, and $\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ pins down the matrix convention. The advice to write basis-state actions is robust across notations.
- **Correctness:** Under the stated basis order and first-qubit control, $\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ is correct.
- **Slight technical refinement:** `block-diagonal form` is accurate, but `familiar` may falsely suggest universality immediately after warning that conventions vary. Drop the adjective or say `under this ordering` again.
- **Pedagogy concern:** The parenthetical definition/cross-reference occupies two lines and openly tells readers they may skim. This supports the case for moving detailed convention examples to the notation page and leaving a compact warning here.
- **Consistency:** Confirm whether Pauli $X$ is genuinely defined in Chapter 4 as stated, not only previewed before its formal Chapter 8 treatment.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** The concrete matrix rewards mathematically prepared readers; unfamiliar readers are given permission to postpone it.

#### “A Note on Conventions” — QFT sign and conversion consequences (lines 353–362)

- **Positive note — unusually precise warning:** The text correctly avoids treating sign as globally SDK-specific, mentions inverse flags, and identifies consequences beyond merely conjugating phase angles.
- **Correctness check:** The displayed negative-exponent transform is a valid unitary DFT/QFT convention. The manuscript must use it consistently in QFT circuits, phase estimation, order finding, and appendices.
- **Probable technical concern — “conjugating controlled-phase angles is the minimum”:** Migrating a circuit between QFT conventions may also involve gate order and swap/bit-reversal conventions; `minimum` is vague and could be interpreted as a sufficient patch. Replace with an explicit non-exhaustive list and a tiny verified circuit identity.
- **Probable technical concern — phase recovery wording:** Swapping QFT/inverse-QFT and reinterpreting phase sign depends on the phase-estimation circuit’s controlled-$U$ convention and eigenphase definition. Later treatment must state those jointly; isolated sign advice is unsafe.
- **Source/readability issue:** The TeX command is split within `\sqrt N`; whitespace is normally tolerated, but breaking commands/arguments across source lines is brittle and hurts maintainability. Keep `$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt N}$` intact.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Experts will appreciate the real implementation warning; novices encounter a dense future concept with no immediate payoff.

#### “A Note on Conventions” — Bloch-sphere scope (lines 364–371)

- **Positive note — excellent metaphor boundary:** The passage states both the exact one-qubit role and the failure of simple multi-qubit generalization. Saying calculations do not depend on the image protects readers who struggle with spatial visualization.
- **Correctness nuance:** Pure one-qubit rays map exactly to the sphere and one-qubit density operators to the ball, while a unitary gate’s action corresponds to a rotation only up to global phase (general channels are affine maps). Since the text says the sphere represents `states and gates`, later material should state these equivalences rather than imply every matrix detail is retained.
- **Accessibility:** Explicitly making visualization optional is strong. Ensure figures do not encode state solely through color or 3D perspective and have text alternatives.
- **Style:** `simple, faithful geometry` is accurate at this level but could be strengthened to `three-dimensional one-to-one geometry`; generalized Bloch vectors can still be faithful algebraic parametrizations despite losing the ball’s simple state-space geometry.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The sphere/ball distinction is a satisfying conceptual fact, and the warning against overextension builds trust.

#### “A Note on the 2026 Timestamp” — mutable metrics and robustness claim (lines 375–385)

- **Positive note — explicit temporal epistemology:** Treating hardware numbers as dated snapshots and designing arguments not to hinge on transient records is exactly the right instinct for a durable book.
- **Strong concern — blanket approximation instruction:** `treat any specific number as approximate` can excuse imprecision and conflates reported values, estimates, ranges, and exact configuration counts. Each number should instead carry a source, measurement/benchmark definition, date, uncertainty or variability where relevant, and status (reported versus independently reproduced).
- **Strong concern — vendor pages as update authority:** Vendor pages are current but not neutral and may silently revise definitions or remove historical results. Cite archived, dated primary technical reports and independent benchmarks where available; offer vendor dashboards only as live supplements.
- **Probable concern — unsupported universal robustness:** `Wherever … load-bearing … survives … an order of magnitude` is an absolute promise that may fail for threshold effects, economic feasibility, error-correction break-even, or algorithmic crossover. Hardware progress is also multidimensional: one metric improving 10× does not preserve conclusions if connectivity, correlated noise, yield, latency, or cost moves differently. Replace the rule with explicit sensitivity analysis appropriate to each argument.
- **Probable concern — one-direction progress assumption:** Figures can worsen under stricter benchmarks or larger systems, and definitions can change. `the figure improving` is too narrow; arguments should survive plausible ranges and explain metric comparability.
- **Edition language:** `being written in 2026` and `printed reference book` sound draft-specific and print-centric. Prefer an edition/revision date and a maintained online errata/update mechanism if available.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The order-of-magnitude thought experiment dramatizes the pace of change, though its confidence exceeds what the policy can guarantee.

#### “A Note on the 2026 Timestamp” — date-dependent feasibility claims (lines 387–392)

- **Positive note — historical framing:** Explicit dates and a warning against reading old feasibility statements in the present tense are responsible and teach readers how to use aging technical material.
- **Audit obligation:** Locate every present-tense feasibility, supremacy/advantage, qubit-count, error-rate, roadmap, access, and market-maturity claim; ensure each has an `as of` date and a durable citation. A section-level date may suffice only if its scope is unmistakable.
- **Probable concern — feasibility is not a single-number predicate:** It depends on device availability, calibration, queue limits, circuit width/depth, shots, compiler, error suppression/mitigation, desired confidence, and cost. Later examples should specify the feasibility criterion, not merely date the conclusion.
- **Optional refinement:** Provide readers a stable updates/errata URL or machine-readable claim ledger. Otherwise the policy explains aging but offers no route to current replacements.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** The five-year-reader scenario is concrete and makes archival value feel intentional.

#### “Acknowledgments” — intellectual sources and citation policy (lines 396–403)

- **Positive note — source lineage:** Naming foundational texts, lecture notes, an algorithm catalogue, and project documentation gives readers a useful picture of the book’s intellectual/tooling inputs.
- **Probable concern — acknowledgments versus bibliography:** This paragraph is primarily a source-method statement, not personal acknowledgment. That is acceptable, but a `Sources and influences` subheading or preface paragraph may set expectations better if no individual/community contributors are acknowledged.
- **Specificity concern:** `the surveys of Michael Nielsen` and `major open-source quantum-software projects` are too vague to verify. Name the works/projects in Appendix D and ensure documentation citations are versioned and attached to the exact behavior claimed.
- **Citation audit obligation:** `particular results, derivations, or examples … citation appears in the chapter` must be reconciled at fine granularity. Standard facts need not be overcited, but adapted examples/derivations require clear provenance and enough marking to distinguish the book’s presentation from a source’s structure.
- **Potential attribution confusion:** Nielsen is named both in Nielsen–Chuang and separately for surveys; this is valid, but readers may benefit from precise titles rather than repeated author identity.

#### “Acknowledgments” — pedagogical influences (lines 405–411)

- **Positive note — cross-disciplinary design:** Looking to machine learning, signal processing, and compilers is well matched to the intended audience and reinforces that quantum computing is being taught as an engineering discipline.
- **Slight suspicion — unsupported broad tradition:** `all of which face the same problem` flattens important differences in prerequisites, empirical practice, and abstraction. `a related problem` is sufficient and more defensible.
- **Probable concern — exercise-design attribution:** The text says only the presence of sanity checks is borrowed, but the earlier no-solutions policy is a distinct and questionable design choice. Cite or explain the evidence for that choice separately; adjacent-field textbooks often do provide answers to selected exercises.

#### “Acknowledgments” — error ownership and issue reporting (lines 413–415)

- **Positive note — invitation to correction:** Owning errors and directing reports to a public tracker supports the living-document model.
- **Usability defect:** `repository's issue tracker` should be a direct link, with guidance for readers of detached PDF/print copies (repository URL, edition/commit, and requested citation details). Do not make them locate the repository indirectly.
- **Maintenance concern:** A living document needs a changelog/version policy so corrections are distinguishable from silent content drift. Connect reported issues to edition timestamps and archived releases.
- **Accessibility/community:** Consider noting an alternative reporting route for readers without an account on the hosting platform and a security/private-contact route if an issue should not be public.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately positive.** The direct personal ownership builds goodwill; the missing link weakens the call to action.

#### “License and Attribution” — operative summary and repository split (lines 419–431)

- **Positive note — unusually readable summary:** The paragraph names the CC license in full, explains attribution/noncommercial/no-derivatives in ordinary language, distinguishes repository tooling, and correctly subordinates the summary to root license files. This is much more useful than a bare badge.
- **Strong legal-precision concern — statutory exceptions:** `any use the CC terms do not grant requires a separate written license` is overbroad because fair use/fair dealing, quotation rights, exhaustion, and other statutory exceptions may permit uses without permission. Add “unless otherwise permitted by applicable law.” This is a textual risk observation, not legal advice; counsel should approve the final wording.
- **Probable legal-precision concern — “any commercial use”:** Copyright licenses regulate particular exclusive rights, not every activity colloquially called use. Merely reading or internally referring to a lawfully obtained copy in a commercial setting may not require a copyright license. Frame the restriction around exercising licensed rights for commercial purposes and defer to the actual license.
- **Positive correctness detail:** The text accurately distinguishes private modification from distribution by saying `distributing modified versions` is prohibited, rather than implying the ND term forbids private changes altogether.
- **Strong scope-consistency check:** The MIT exception is described as code, reusable infrastructure, companion programs, tooling, and process documentation. Reconcile that prose with the actual repository licensing matrix, including README files, configuration, metadata, figures, and non-book prose. A binary rule such as `book/** under CC; everything else under MIT` would be far easier to apply if that is the intended root policy.
- **Usability defect:** `LICENSE` and `LICENSE-MIT` should be direct links in digital editions and printed as a durable repository URL/edition reference elsewhere. Detached readers cannot inspect a repository-root file by name alone.
- **Terminology suspicion:** `dual-licensed` usually means the same work is offered under two alternative licenses. Here the paragraph also describes different repository components under different licenses plus separately negotiated permissions. Clarify whether the book itself is genuinely dual-licensed (CC plus a commercial proprietary option) and call the repository arrangement a split licensing policy.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Legal material is necessarily interruptive, but the concrete permissions and plain language make it unusually approachable.

#### “License and Attribution” — policy intent and permission examples (lines 433–442)

- **Positive note — concrete scenarios:** Course packs, training, translations, and commercial printing help readers understand when to contact the author. Explicitly noting that translation is an adaptation is informative.
- **Precision concern — “free to read/study/recommend”:** These phrases describe intent but not the licensed acts involved. Recommending costs nothing regardless; redistributing a copy is what the CC license addresses. Consider “free of charge to access, and share verbatim for noncommercial purposes with attribution.”
- **Probable concern — exclusivity claim:** CC BY-NC-ND still permits noncommercial verbatim printed copies, so a future edition has commercial exclusivity at most, not print exclusivity generally. State `commercial printed-edition rights` to avoid contradiction with the permission just summarized.
- **Tone/readability:** The em-dash interruption explaining `free of charge` is necessary because `free` is overloaded, but the sentence remains long and defensive. Two sentences—intent, then retained rights—would be clearer.
- **Usability defect:** `please get in touch` provides no link or address. Add a durable licensing-contact method and expected information (use, territory/audience, format), including an alternative to a public issue.
- **Legal-maintenance note:** Because license summaries can create reliance even when disclaimed, run automated wording/link checks and obtain qualified review after every material licensing change.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Explaining the author’s publishing rationale humanizes restrictive terms; readers primarily seeking content may still find the detail long for a preface.

#### Closing transition, divider, and repeated navigation (lines 444–450)

- **Positive note — forward transition:** The closing sentence tells readers what practical value comes next, and the repeated navigation means a 450-line page ends with an immediate action.
- **Consistency defect:** `the next chapter` again refers to a front-matter self-check that the book’s own chapter count appears not to include. Use `next section/page` unless it is formally a numbered chapter.
- **Slight suspicion — “hard look”:** Energetic but vague; `a concrete diagnostic` is more specific. The nearby `concrete self-check items` already supplies that clarity.
- **Navigation consistency:** The bottom navigation exactly matches the top, which is good. Retain automatic generation or validate both copies so titles/order cannot diverge.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderately high.** The phrase `With those preliminaries out of the way` provides closure and restores momentum after licensing material.

#### File-level synthesis — `00-preface.md`

- **Overall assessment:** The preface has a strong, candid voice and a valuable editorial contract: mathematically serious, engineering-aware, skeptical of hype, practical about reading modes, explicit about conventions, and honest about temporal decay. Its best moments are memorable without sacrificing purpose. The dominant weaknesses are overbroad binaries, several unnecessary audience gates, ambitious absolute promises, and navigation paths that sometimes violate the dependency philosophy they advertise.
- **Highest-priority corrections within this file:** (1) repair the legal-summary exceptions and clarify the repository licensing boundary; (2) rebuild and validate the hardware and fastest reading paths so prerequisites precede dependents; (3) replace strongly typed/build-system gates with transferable software skills; (4) decompose the Qiskit bit-order explanation into quantum/classical/register layers with a verified example; (5) qualify the no-forward-reference, current-era, software-convergence, paper-reading, and 10×-robustness claims.
- **Pedagogical trajectory:** The preface generally reduces uncertainty, but it alternates between welcoming experienced developers and screening them via requirements unrelated to the actual subject. Its repeated convention/detail previews also impose substantial quantum-specific cognitive load before Chapter 1. Consolidation into canonical references plus short warnings would improve pacing.
- **Entertainment verdict:** **Good overall (roughly 7/10 for technical front matter).** The hype/dismissal hook, failed-analogy line, concrete professional examples, and sharp editorial maxims keep a long preface readable. Engagement drops during duplicated organizational guidance, renderer internals, dense endianness detail, and extended licensing rationale.
- **Open cross-book checks created:** preface promise coverage; exact prerequisite graph and absence of required forward dependencies; reading-path executability; exercise/answer policy; boldface-to-glossary reconciliation; convention agreement across three locations; QFT/endianness consistency; mutable-claim dating and sensitivity; citation/provenance completeness; stable cross-references; status-banner consistency; license-boundary/link consistency; and availability/access assumptions in hands-on work.
