- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.5/10.** The use cases are intrinsically vivid, but repeated caveats and a foggy platform ranking blunt the energy.

## Second-pass ledger — `book/part-04-gates-and-circuits/09-quantum-circuits.md` — §9.9 Classical Feedforward (lines 100–106)

### Heading and relation to §9.8 (line 100)

- **Good sequencing:** §9.8 names the capability and §9.9 opens the control loop in detail.
- **Potential redundancy:** Line 96 already defines feedforward. Either make that sentence a one-line preview and let this section own the definition, or merge the two sections.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** A control-loop framing promises concrete machinery.

### “Measure → classical computation → apply” loop (line 102, opening)

- **Strong compact definition:** The arrow chain is memorable and captures canonical active feedforward.
- **Not always literally a loop:** A single measurement-conditioned operation is a causal chain; “loop” suggests iteration. Dynamic circuits may branch without looping, and feedback loops may repeat.
- **Broader action space:** The controller may update a frame, choose a basis/parameter, route a carrier, accept/abort, or schedule another measurement rather than apply a quantum gate.
- **Data path:** Useful decomposition: acquire/ discriminate readout → move/store bits → compute predicate/decoder result → dispatch timed conditional action.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Excellent.** The arrows give the section kinetic energy.

### “Must complete within the coherence time” (line 102)

- **Too categorical:** The deadline is the protocol’s allowable measurement-to-dependent-action latency, which may be constrained by decoherence of live quantum data, total logical-cycle time, memory errors, or throughput—not necessarily one bare-qubit coherence time.
- **Deferred-action exception:** Pauli-frame updates and terminal reinterpretation can record the result now and postpone physical correction; no immediate gate need complete within `$T_1$`/`$T_2$` in those cases.
- **Protected-memory exception:** Error-corrected/logical qubits do not have the same deadline as a single physical qubit, though decoder backlog and logical-cycle latency still matter.
- **Coherence is gradual:** `$T_1$` and `$T_2$` are exponential timescales, not hard expiry timestamps. Required latency depends on acceptable added error.
- **Parallel work:** Classical processing can sometimes overlap unrelated quantum operations; OpenQASM 3 explicitly contemplates concurrent external computation.
- **Recommended:** “For latency-sensitive branches, the measurement-to-action path must fit within the protocol’s coherence and error budget.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High stakes**, currently taught as a misleading cliff.

### “Superconducting devices ... 100 μs” (line 102)

- **Unstable generalization:** Coherence varies by device, qubit, metric, calibration, operating point, and date. `$T_1$`, Ramsey `$T_2^*$`, echo `$T_2$`, and effective idle error are not interchangeable.
- **Current contradiction:** IBM reported a median `$T_1$` of 350 μs for its first Nighthawk in January 2026, while also saying dynamic circuits were not yet supported and mid-circuit-measurement quality was limited. High coherence and feedforward availability are separate axes.
- **Precision:** If retaining a number, name the system, metric, statistic, date, and source. Otherwise say “often tens to hundreds of microseconds” as an explicitly rough scale, then avoid building an exact latency argument on it.
- **Formatting defect:** Source contains `$100\\,\mu\mathrm{s}$`; the doubled backslash before the thin-space command appears likely to produce a line break or malformed math rather than `100\,\mu\mathrm{s}`. Verify renderer output.
- **Source checked 22 July 2026:** [IBM Nighthawk/Heron announcement](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/announcements/en/product-updates/2026-01-05-nighthawk).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Concrete numbers help**, but a floating unsourced number ages into misinformation.

### Kernel/userspace round-trip comparison (line 102)

- **Category is underspecified:** A “typical” kernel/userspace round trip is not inherently millisecond-scale; system calls and context transitions can be microseconds or below, while networked cloud job/control round trips can be milliseconds or much longer.
- **Likely intended contrast:** Host-mediated interactive control through an operating system/network/service stack is much slower and less deterministic than an embedded real-time controller near the QPU.
- **Determinism matters:** Worst-case/jitter and scheduled timing can matter as much as mean latency.
- **Recommended:** Replace the dubious OS microbenchmark with “ordinary host/cloud control paths are generally too slow and nondeterministic for tight in-circuit feedback.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Vivid analogy**, factually foggy enough to distract technical readers.

### Dedicated controller and restricted instruction set (line 102, close)

- **Broadly correct:** Real-time feedback generally depends on specialized low-latency hardware/firmware and a target-supported subset of classical operations.
- **Language versus target:** A source language may express more than a backend implements. OpenQASM 3 explicitly says compilers may reject runtime operations unsupported by the target.
- **Current concrete example:** IBM’s current dynamic-circuit guide says OpenQASM 3 defines multiple flow structures while the relevant runtime path supports conditional `if`; availability and instruction details remain backend/version-specific.
- **Layering:** Distinguish language syntax, SDK IR, compiler lowering, controller ISA, firmware scheduling, and exposed QPU capability.
- **Sources checked 22 July 2026:** [OpenQASM 3 classical instructions](https://openqasm.com/versions/3.0/language/classical.html); [IBM dynamic-circuit execution guide](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/execute-dynamic-circuits).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high practical insight.** This deserves a small stack diagram or table.

### “Three canonical uses” framing (line 104)

- **Good signposting:** The triplet moves from gate injection to QEC to adaptive computation.
- **Not exhaustive:** State preparation, qubit reuse, repeat-until-success, active leakage removal, entanglement swapping, and heralding are also canonical; “three important uses” is safer.
- **Granularity imbalance:** The QEC item is much denser than the adaptive-protocol item.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High**, because examples rapidly widen the reader’s horizon.

### Teleportation-based `$T$` gates (line 104, first example)

- **Essential idea correct:** Fault-tolerant `$T$` implementation commonly consumes an injected/distilled magic state and uses measurement-dependent Clifford handling.
- **Protocol dependence:** Exact ancilla state, CNOT orientation, measurement basis, outcome convention, and whether the correction is `$S$`, `$S^\dagger$`, or a tracked Clifford depend on the injection circuit. “In many surface-code schemes” helps but is still loose.
- **Terminology:** This is usually called magic-state injection/gate teleportation; name it so readers can search for the construction.
- **Not merely Pauli—good point:** Highlighting a conditional Clifford is pedagogically valuable because it explains why a Pauli frame alone may be insufficient.
- **Forward-reference load:** Chapter 19 is far away. Include one sentence defining a magic state operationally, not only parenthetically as “specially prepared.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional teaser.** It makes fault tolerance feel less abstract.

### Conditional `$S$` correction claim (line 104)

- **Needs an explicit circuit or convention:** Without the injection diagram, readers cannot verify which measurement result triggers which correction or why `$S$` appears.
- **Clifford-frame nuance:** Some architectures track the conditional Clifford in a richer frame, adapt subsequent measurements, or use selective teleportation rather than immediately execute `$S$`.
- **Scope:** “Not merely a Pauli” is true for common `$T$` injection, not a universal statement about every teleportation-based logical-gate scheme.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High surprise**, but risks becoming trivia without the mechanism.

### Error-correction use claim (line 104, second example)

- **Core point sound:** Repeated stabilizer/syndrome extraction creates classical data that decoders use to infer likely errors or logical observables.
- **“Every cycle ... applies corrections” is inaccurate:** Many QEC implementations do not physically correct each cycle. They update a Pauli frame or maintain a decoding history; even decoder output may arrive after later cycles.
- **Syndrome versus raw outcomes:** A syndrome/detection event is often a parity/change derived from multiple measurement results, not simply “the syndrome bits” emitted directly.
- **Temporal decoding:** Fault-tolerant decoding commonly uses a space-time history of repeated rounds, not an independent per-cycle map from one syndrome to one correction.
- **Measurement errors:** Repetition is crucial precisely because a single round’s outcomes can be faulty.
- **Better:** “Each extraction cycle produces measurement data; a decoder processes the evolving syndrome history and updates a frame or schedules any required physical action.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high importance**, but the current sentence reinforces the beginner myth of immediate correction.

### Pauli-frame explanation (line 104)

- **Excellent inclusion:** Avoiding physical Pauli gates reduces latency/error and is central to realistic fault-tolerant control.
- **“Software-tracked” can mislead:** Tracking may occur in tightly coupled FPGA/ASIC/firmware/control systems rather than ordinary software; “classically tracked” is safer.
- **Frame propagation:** One commutes/propagates the frame through later Clifford operations by updating its classical description; no quantum gate need occur.
- **When it becomes relevant:** A non-Clifford gate may promote a Pauli frame to a Clifford correction/adaptive choice, but “physically relevant” is not always synonymous with applying a gate. Measurement outcomes can instead be reinterpreted or bases adapted.
- **Decoder latency caveat:** Delayed frame resolution can be tolerated until a dependent non-Clifford operation/measurement deadline, motivating “reaction time,” not merely per-cycle decoding speed.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional.** This is precisely the kind of counterintuitive engineering fact readers remember.

### Adaptive protocols and photonic routing (line 104, third example)

- **Correct broad use:** Measurement-based quantum computation changes later measurement bases based on earlier outcomes; linear-optical schemes use detection records for routing, switching, correction, or heralding.
- **“Route between alternative branches” is vague:** Branching may be logical basis/angle selection rather than physically routing photons.
- **MBQC mechanism:** Byproduct operators accumulate, and feedforward adapts later measurement angles/bases to preserve the intended logical computation.
- **Photonic qualification:** Distinguish active real-time feedforward from postselection; the latter filters runs after the fact and is not feedforward.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High**, though one concrete miniature example would outperform the abstraction.

### Cost and benchmarking transition (line 106, opening)

- **Unsupported claim:** “Increasingly visible in benchmarks” needs a named benchmark and metric—measurement-to-action latency, dynamic-circuit layer error, conditional fidelity, throughput, or application-level success.
- **Cost dimensions:** Add readout time/error, controller latency/jitter, idle decoherence, branch imbalance/padding, conditional gate error, compilation restrictions, and unavailable optimization passes.
- **Positive counterpoint:** Feedforward may reduce quantum depth/width or avoid coherent multi-qubit control; net cost is workload-dependent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Promising hook**, currently no payoff because no benchmark follows.

### Vendor terminology list (line 106)

- **Useful search guidance:** “conditional gate,” “if statement,” and “real-time classical control” help readers navigate documentation.
- **Terminology instability:** Also “dynamic circuits,” “fast feedback,” “active reset,” and “measurement-conditioned operation.” Names are not semantically identical.
- **Capability warning:** A documented `if` syntax does not prove hardware execution, arbitrary classical computation, low latency, or support on every backend.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High practical utility.** A boxed “documentation search terms” note could work well.

### OpenQASM 3 claim (line 106)

- **Broadly correct:** OpenQASM 3 introduced explicit classical scalar/data types, expressions, branching, loops, functions, and timing-oriented constructs beyond OpenQASM 2’s narrow condition.
- **Version precision:** “OpenQASM 3” is a version family/live specification; cite the exact specification version used, because features such as `switch` evolved after 3.0 (where keywords were reserved) into the live spec.
- **Expressibility versus realizability:** The specification explicitly permits a compiler to reject runtime operations unsupported by the target. The manuscript should say this immediately after the feature claim.
- **First-class wording:** Fine conversationally, but enumerate one or two concrete types/control constructs for readers unfamiliar with language-design jargon.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate-to-high**, especially for readers who want to program devices.

### OpenQASM 2 restricted conditional (line 106, close)

- **Substantively correct:** OpenQASM 2’s built-in conditional form compares an entire classical register with a nonnegative integer and conditionally executes one quantum operation.
- **Important restrictions:** It is not a general block-structured `if`, does not directly express arbitrary Boolean expressions, and the comparison semantics involve the register’s integer interpretation/width.
- **Code formatting good:** `` `if (creg == int)` `` is compact, but it looks like literal grammar metavariables; label it schematic syntax.
- **Comparison opportunity:** A two-row 2.0 versus 3.x table would make the evolution instantly legible and keep backend-support caveats visible.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High historical/programming value**, abrupt as the section’s final sentence.

### §9.9 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section connects low-latency control to magic-state injection, QEC decoding, Pauli frames, and adaptive computation in only three paragraphs.
- **Highest-severity defects:** “Must complete within the coherence time,” a generic 100 μs superconducting value, millisecond “kernel/userspace round-trips,” and “every cycle ... applies corrections” are all materially overgeneralized or inaccurate.
- **Main structural repair:** Separate the physical measurement-to-action pipeline from language expressibility and backend implementation; give exact dated examples and a latency/error-budget model.
- **Main pedagogical repair:** Explain that QEC usually tracks inferred corrections across syndrome history rather than physically correcting after every round.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.0/10.** Dense with memorable real-world ideas; precision repairs would turn it into a standout section.

## Second-pass ledger — `book/part-04-gates-and-circuits/09-quantum-circuits.md` — §9.10 Circuit Depth (lines 108–116)

### Heading (line 108)

- **Necessary topic:** Depth is a foundational circuit-complexity measure and belongs near width, scheduling, and hardware execution.
- **Placement question:** Depth was already used informally in earlier chapters; consider defining size, width, logical depth, and duration together before hardware-specific claims.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Familiar concept, but lower bounds and parallelism can make it vivid.

### “Length of the longest path” definition (line 110, opening)

- **Correct for a fixed unit-duration dependency DAG:** Depth is the maximum number of gate vertices/layers on a dependency path under the chosen gate set and parallelism rules.
- **Gate-model dependence:** Decomposing one gate changes the DAG and depth. State the primitive gate set, allowed connectivity, and whether measurements/classical operations count.
- **Path convention:** If vertices are gates, clarify whether depth counts vertices or edges; otherwise an empty circuit and a one-gate circuit create off-by-one ambiguity.
- **Dynamic circuits:** Branches, loops, probabilistic stopping, and feedforward need worst-case, expected, branch-conditioned, or scheduled duration—not one static DAG depth.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High clarity** if the model assumptions appear in the same sentence.

### Packed-layer equivalence (line 110)

- **Valid under unit durations and only qubit/dependency exclusions:** Minimum layer count equals critical-path length for a fixed DAG when every operation takes one slot and there are no extra resource constraints.
- **Not merely “packed tightly”:** An arbitrary greedy packing need not define the minimum depth once routing, crosstalk exclusions, shared controls, limited parallel entanglers, classical-resource constraints, or variable durations enter.
- **Commutation freedom:** A compiler may reorder commuting gates or rewrite the circuit, changing dependencies beyond those in the original textual order.
- **Terminology:** Distinguish **logical depth** (layer count), **weighted depth/critical-path duration**, and actual scheduled makespan.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate**, but a three-gate counterexample/diagram would make it concrete.

### “Depth is the relevant time-cost metric” (line 110)

- **Overstatement:** Unweighted depth is a proxy, not the hardware time-cost metric. Gates, measurement, reset, delay, movement, and feedforward have heterogeneous durations.
- **Hardware constraints:** Routing SWAPs, limited simultaneous drive/readout resources, frequency collisions, crosstalk avoidance, calibration rules, and synchronization can lengthen a schedule without changing abstract dependency depth.
- **Other relevant costs:** Shot count, initialization/readout, classical latency, queueing, compilation, batch throughput, and error-correction cycles affect wall-clock/application cost.
- **Better:** “Depth is a central abstract time-complexity measure; after assigning operation durations and hardware constraints, scheduled critical-path duration is the closer per-shot hardware metric.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High practical relevance**, currently too absolute.

### “Sets wall-clock duration of one run” (line 110)

- **Incorrect literally:** A depth-10 circuit with ten 20 ns single-qubit layers and one with ten microsecond-scale measurement/reset layers do not have the same duration.
- **Per-run ambiguity:** Hardware execution may include reset, readout, control-program overhead, repetition delay, dynamical-decoupling pulses, error-correction cycles, and conditional branch padding.
- **Probabilistic execution:** Branching/repeat-until-success produces a duration distribution rather than one deterministic value.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low trust risk:** hardware readers will immediately object.

### “Must fit inside coherence time” (line 110, close)

- **Same hard-deadline misconception as §9.9:** `$T_1$`/`$T_2$` are decay scales, not deadlines; accumulated error grows continuously and depends on state, idling, control, and mitigation.
- **Not all qubits live for full circuit:** Individual qubit lifetimes run from preparation/first use to measurement/reset; mid-circuit reuse changes the relevant intervals.
- **Fault-tolerant circuits:** Logical computation can far exceed physical coherence times through repeated error correction, provided logical error rates/resources suffice.
- **Better:** “In uncorrected hardware, longer live intervals generally increase decoherence; schedules must meet the application’s fidelity budget.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Dramatic but misleading** as written.

### Disjoint-gate parallelism example (line 112, opening)

- **Correct in the abstract circuit model:** `$n$` independent one-qubit gates can occupy one layer.
- **Width notation:** “Width-$n$ circuit” is understandable but define width as number of wires/qubits, not number of simultaneously active gates.
- **Hardware caveat:** Simultaneous execution may be restricted or have different calibrated error than isolated gates; abstract depth remains one even if the physical scheduler serializes subsets.
- **Initial state convention:** If no gate is required, preparation of `$|0^n\rangle$` may have depth zero rather than one; the example itself does use `$n$` gates.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High pedagogical utility.** Crisp correction to naïve gate counting.

### Shared-qubit serialization (line 112)

- **Correct standard rule:** Two ordinary gates cannot simultaneously act on the same qubit in the circuit model.
- **Dependency nuance:** Textual sharing creates an ordering, but adjacent gates may sometimes combine/cancel into one native operation under optimization.
- **Non-overlap not sufficient physically:** Disjoint qubit sets can still conflict through controls/crosstalk/readout buses.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate**, clear and necessary.

### ASAP scheduler definition (line 112)

- **Broadly correct:** “As soon as possible” scheduling assigns each operation its earliest legal start after predecessors/resources permit.
- **Layers versus time:** With heterogeneous durations it schedules start times, not merely discrete layers.
- **Fixed-DAG special case:** For a DAG with unit-duration operations and no resource constraints beyond dependencies already encoded, earliest-start scheduling reaches the critical-path makespan; calling it merely “near-optimal” undersells that restricted case.
- **General case:** With shared-resource constraints, routing choices, crosstalk exclusions, or alternative decompositions, greedy ASAP can be suboptimal and may optimize makespan at the expense of idle exposure/noise.
- **ALAP counterpart:** Mention as-late-as-possible scheduling; intentional delays and dynamical decoupling mean earliest is not always best for fidelity.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High practical compiler insight**, deserving one miniature schedule.

### “Modulo gate-duration heterogeneity” (line 112, close)

- **Incomplete qualifier:** Heterogeneous durations can be handled by weighted critical paths; the harder gaps are resource conflicts, topology/routing, commutation/resynthesis choices, calibration constraints, and branch timing.
- **“Near-optimal” lacks guarantee:** State whether this is heuristic experience or a theorem under specified assumptions.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate**, currently reads as hand-waving over the important part.

### Lower-bound transition (line 114, opening)

- **Good escalation:** Moving from scheduling examples to causal lower bounds gives depth conceptual weight.
- **Define asymptotics:** Specify the architecture family, local gate arity/range, and what approximation/error is allowed as `$n$` grows.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Impossibility results naturally create intrigue.

### GHZ nearest-neighbor lower bound (line 114)

- **Correct order under standard assumptions:** On a 1D nearest-neighbor architecture with bounded-range two-qubit gates and product input, correlating endpoints/GHZ preparation requires `$\Omega(n)$` depth by a light-cone argument; a CNOT chain gives `$O(n)$`.
- **Architecture wording:** “Nearest-neighbor architectures” is too broad. In a 2D grid, diameter is `$\Theta(\sqrt n)$`; in a `$D$`-dimensional local lattice it scales roughly as `$n^{1/D}$`, not always `$n$`.
- **Measurements/communication caveat:** Pre-shared entanglement, nonlocal classical feedforward, teleportation, movement, or different primitives change the bound/resource accounting.
- **Approximation:** Exact preparation and constant-error approximate preparation may require separately stated bounds.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional** if the light-cone picture is drawn.

### “Any state with correlations spanning the full register” (line 114)

- **Too vague and likely false under natural readings:** A 1D cluster/graph state can be prepared from `$|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$` with constant-depth layers of nearest-neighbor CZ gates, yet it is globally entangled and colloquially has correlations “spanning” the register.
- **Needed property:** State a precise endpoint correlation, connected correlator, recoverable information, circuit complexity, or long-range-entanglement criterion whose light cones force the bound.
- **Entanglement is insufficient:** Global/multipartite entanglement alone does not imply linear preparation depth in a local geometry.
- **Severity:** **Strong conceptual overgeneralization.** Keep GHZ as the clean example rather than claiming all globally correlated states.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High idea**, dangerous phrase.

### Product-state contrast (line 114)

- **Mostly correct:** Any specified tensor product of arbitrary one-qubit pure states can be prepared in one parallel layer if arbitrary one-qubit gates are primitives.
- **Conventions:** `$|0^n\rangle$` itself needs depth zero from the stated input; restricted discrete gate sets may require synthesis depth for each factor, though still parallel across qubits.
- **Mixed product states:** Preparation may require noise, reset, ancillas, or randomization; likely outside intended scope.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Good contrast**, but say “arbitrary pure product states with native one-qubit preparation.”

### Fully connected GHZ upper bound (line 114)

- **Correct:** A binary fanout tree of parallel CNOTs doubles the entangled set each layer, giving `$O(\log n)$` depth with all-to-all connectivity and disjoint-gate constraints.
- **Matching lower bound:** With bounded-arity gates and product input, each qubit’s influence cone can grow only exponentially with depth, giving `$\Omega(\log n)$`; thus `$\Theta(\log n)$` is the stronger instructive statement.
- **Not constant despite all-to-all:** One control cannot participate in many two-qubit gates simultaneously under the standard model. A native unbounded fanout/multiqubit entangler would change this.
- **“Some families like” is weak:** Name GHZ specifically and give the doubling construction.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** A satisfying geometry-versus-depth payoff.

### Fault-tolerant Clifford+`$T$` synthesis factor (line 114)

- **Directionally correct:** Approximating arbitrary continuous rotations over a discrete fault-tolerant gate set introduces accuracy-dependent sequence length, commonly logarithmic in `$1/\epsilon$` for efficient/near-optimal single-qubit synthesis.
- **Undefined exponent:** `$O(\log^c(1/\epsilon))$` with unspecified `$c$` is too foggy after §8.11. State the algorithm/model and exponent or use `$O(\log(1/\epsilon))$` where justified.
- **Cost metric distinction:** `$T$` count, `$T$` depth, Clifford count, ancilla count, magic-state factory throughput, and online depth can scale differently. “Discrete gates” hides the dominant resource.
- **Parallel synthesis:** Per-rotation gate count does not automatically multiply total circuit depth if rotations occur concurrently.
- **Approximation allocation:** For many rotations, per-gate error must be chosen relative to the total allowed algorithmic error; using the same `$\epsilon$` for each may not control global error.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High importance**, too compressed for one clause.

### “Inflating gate count everywhere” (line 114)

- **Overstatement:** Only non-native continuous rotations requiring approximation incur this factor; Clifford gates and exactly synthesizable angles do not.
- **Compiler effects:** Cancellation, phase-polynomial optimization, repeat-angle reuse, ancilla-assisted methods, or probabilistic synthesis can alter counts.
- **Critical-path qualification is good:** The text correctly notes that depth grows only where synthesized rotations lie on the critical path, but that clashes with “everywhere.”
- **Better:** “inflating the count of approximated rotations and the depth of any synthesized sequences on the critical path.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate**, dense enough to cause rereading.

### Schematic overall complexity product (line 114)

- **Insufficiently founded:** `$O(\mathrm{poly}(n)\log^c(1/\epsilon))$` assumes a polynomial number/depth of relevant rotations and a uniform accuracy allocation; many algorithms have different dependence on problem size, simulation time, condition number, precision, or number of rotations.
- **Two-layer explanation helps:** Saying the factors arise at algorithm and compilation layers is pedagogically useful.
- **Variable collision risk:** Algorithmic target accuracy, per-rotation synthesis error, and total trace/operator error should not all be called `$\epsilon$` without a budget relation.
- **Recommendation:** Present as a toy composition example with explicit premises, not a generic form for “many practical algorithms.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low-to-moderate.** Symbolic fog interrupts the otherwise intuitive section.

### NISQ/native continuous-gate contrast (line 114, close)

- **Broadly correct:** Calibrated parameterized rotations do not require Clifford+`$T$` digital approximation, so the same discrete-synthesis sequence-length dependence is absent.
- **But compilation still approximates:** Native gate restrictions, pulse discretization, angle resolution, calibration models, composite pulses, and decomposition of non-native two-qubit operations can introduce other precision/cost relations.
- **“Pulse-level” wording:** Some cloud services no longer expose pulse-level control even though calibrated pulse implementations exist internally; distinguish physical implementation from user access.
- **NISQ/fault-tolerant dichotomy is imperfect:** Early logical/fault-tolerant architectures may expose analog rotations through special protocols, while NISQ compilers can target discrete native subsets.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Good practical contrast**, needs one sentence of nuance.

### GHZ-state figure reference (line 116)

- **Caption content:** Correctly describes a three-qubit H-plus-CNOT-chain circuit and ties the drawing to linear nearest-neighbor scaling.
- **Scaling mismatch:** A three-qubit image alone cannot visually demonstrate asymptotic growth; add an `$n$`-wire schematic or a small 3/5/7-qubit sequence.
- **Alternative comparison:** Show linear-chain GHZ beside binary-tree all-to-all GHZ to make `$O(n)$` versus `$O(\log n)$` immediate.
- **Accessibility:** Alt text is substantive, but should state wire order/control-target symbols if the SVG is not available.
- **Deferred asset audit:** `book/part-04-gates-and-circuits/figures/ghz-state.svg` will be inspected structurally and visually in its own one-file pass.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High potential.** Comparative diagrams would deliver the section’s best insight.

### §9.10 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** Disjoint-gate examples and GHZ propagation make abstract depth tangible.
- **Highest-severity defects:** Unweighted depth does not set wall-clock duration; “nearest-neighbor” does not universally imply `$\Omega(n)$`; and “any state with correlations spanning the full register” is undefined/false under common interpretations.
- **Main repair:** Define logical depth, weighted critical-path duration, and scheduled hardware makespan separately, then state light-cone bounds for a precise geometry and correlation task.
- **Compression concern:** The final paragraph combines geometry lower bounds, product states, all-to-all GHZ, fault-tolerant synthesis, global error allocation, and NISQ compilation. Split it into at least two subsections.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.6/10.** Parallelism and causal cones are inherently engaging; the synthesis-complexity tail becomes overly compressed.

## Second-pass ledger — `book/part-04-gates-and-circuits/09-quantum-circuits.md` — §9.11 Circuit Width (lines 118–124)

### Heading (line 118)

- **Natural pairing:** Width follows depth and prepares the topology discussion well.
- **Opportunity:** Introduce space, time, and space-time volume as a coordinated trio rather than two isolated scalar metrics.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate.** Resource tradeoffs can raise it above a glossary entry.

### Width definition (line 120, opening)

- **Definitional ambiguity/likely defect:** Standard circuit width is normally the number of qubit wires/qubits used by the circuit, or maximum number of live qubits in a dynamic allocation model—not “the number of qubits it acts on simultaneously.”
- **Simultaneity confusion:** A width-100 circuit may apply a gate to only one qubit in a given layer. Conversely, “acts on simultaneously” sounds like layer occupancy or parallel gate support.
- **Static versus dynamic models:** In a fixed-wire circuit diagram, width is simply wire count even while wires idle. With reset/reuse/dynamic allocation, define **peak live physical qubits** separately from total logical lifetimes/roles.
- **Input/output convention:** Complexity theory sometimes distinguishes input width, ancilla/workspace, and total circuit width; say what is counted, including classical bits if relevant.
- **Better:** “For a fixed-wire circuit, width is the number of qubit wires. In a model with allocation and reuse, the analogous hardware requirement is the maximum number of qubits simultaneously live.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High clarity payoff** once the terms are separated.

### “For most algorithms, width equals register size” (line 120)

- **Tautological/underspecified:** “The qubit register” often means all wires, making the equality true by definition; an algorithm may have input, output, work, magic-state, syndrome, and communication registers.
- **Algorithm versus implementation:** Width belongs to a particular circuit/implementation, not uniquely to an abstract algorithm. Different decompositions and ancilla strategies yield different width.
- **Multiple registers:** Register partitioning is a naming/type convenience and need not affect physical width.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low.** Replace with a concrete input-plus-workspace formula.

### Reused ancillae and “qubit-roles” (line 120, close)

- **Good conceptual distinction:** One physical carrier can serve multiple sequential logical lifetimes after disentanglement/measurement/reset.
- **Role metric needs definition:** “Total number of qubit-roles played” is not standard. It may mean logical variables, allocation events, wire segments, or lifetime intervals.
- **Reuse prerequisites:** A qubit must be safely released—uncomputed/decoupled or measured/reset according to semantics—before reassignment.
- **Peak-live analogy:** This resembles register allocation/liveness analysis in classical compilers; the analogy could make the idea immediately intuitive.
- **Ancilla spelling:** The manuscript uses “ancillae”; ensure book-wide consistency with “ancillas.” Both occur in technical writing, but mixed usage is distracting.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** The compiler-register analogy is an engaging missed opportunity.

### “Width and depth trade off” (line 122, opening)

- **Useful heuristic, not universal law:** Some circuits can improve both via optimization; some have independent lower bounds; adding ancillas does not necessarily reduce critical depth.
- **Pareto framing:** Say implementations often exhibit a width–depth tradeoff and should be compared on a Pareto frontier.
- **Other axes:** Gate count, `$T$` count/depth, connectivity, classical latency, error, communication, and magic-state throughput may dominate.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** A genuine design tension gives the section narrative force.

### Wide/shallow implementation (line 122)

- **Broadly correct pattern:** Extra workspace can parallelize arithmetic, fanout classical-basis controls, store intermediate values, or avoid serial recomputation.
- **Not merely flattening the dependency DAG:** Ancillas can change the algorithm/circuit DAG through alternative decompositions; adding idle wires alone does nothing.
- **No-cloning boundary:** Extra ancillas cannot freely duplicate arbitrary unknown quantum data. Parallelization techniques must use allowed entanglement, basis-encoded data, or recomputation.
- **Physical penalty:** More qubits can increase routing, crosstalk, calibration burden, syndrome overhead, and failure opportunities.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High**, especially with a reversible-computation example.

### Narrow/deep via reuse and uncomputation (line 122)

- **Directionally sound:** Serializing workspace and recomputing/uncomputing intermediates can reduce peak live width.
- **Conflated mechanisms:** Uncomputation releases coherent workspace without measurement; measurement/reset releases qubits nonunitarily where semantics permit. Treat separately.
- **Time cost can be gate count and depth:** Reversible pebbling often trades space for recomputation time; the exact curve can be nontrivial rather than one extra layer.
- **Measurement-assisted uncomputation:** Some structured garbage can be erased with measurement and classically controlled corrections, changing the tradeoff.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high intellectual potential.** Reversible pebble games would make a compelling aside.

### “Right operating point” (line 122)

- **Correct engineering framing:** Resource availability and workload constraints determine the useful implementation.
- **Not simply whichever resource is scarcer:** Optimize expected successful-result cost/fidelity/throughput under coupled constraints. Extra depth consumes coherence and error budget; extra width may shorten duration.
- **Hardware availability:** Connectivity and native operations mean the same nominal width/depth can compile very differently.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High practical trust.** Add “Pareto-optimal under the target error model.”

### Small-NISQ “narrow circuits win” claim (line 122)

- **Overcategorical and potentially wrong:** If a circuit does not fit, narrowing may be necessary; if it already fits, added depth can sharply lower fidelity and make the narrow version worse.
- **Feasibility versus optimality:** Width is a hard capacity constraint, while depth is often a soft but severe error constraint. First require fit, then compare fidelity/runtime.
- **Qubit quality/topology:** Using fewer but worse-connected qubits can add SWAPs; using more high-quality qubits can reduce depth and error.
- **Mid-circuit overhead:** Reuse may add slow/noisy measurement and reset, making a wider circuit preferable even on a small device.
- **Better:** “When the wider circuit exceeds capacity, reuse may be the only feasible option; among fitting circuits, the best width–depth point is hardware- and noise-dependent.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Punchy but misleading.** The hard-versus-soft constraint distinction is more satisfying.

### Fault-tolerant logical-width claim (line 122, close)

- **Correct important pressure:** One logical qubit can require many physical data/syndrome qubits, so logical width is expensive.
- **Patch is architecture-specific:** “Large patch” describes surface/topological codes, not all fault-tolerant schemes. Say “for example, a surface-code patch.”
- **Time is expensive too:** Longer logical depth increases code cycles, accumulated logical failure, and factory/runtime demand. Space-time volume is often the more revealing metric.
- **Factories dominate:** Magic-state factories may consume more physical qubits than the algorithm’s data register; “width” should include them if estimating machine resources.
- **Dynamic resource sharing:** Factories, routing space, buffers, lattice surgery, and decoder hardware complicate a single logical-qubit count.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high glimpse of scale**, deserving a quantified later example.

### Related-metrics transition (line 124)

- **Good instinct:** Separating nearby concepts is precisely what the opening definition needs.
- **But terms are nonstandard/undefined:** “Register count,” “simultaneous gate slots,” and “effective qubit reuse rate” need formulas, use cases, and units.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low-to-moderate** because the list feels appended rather than developed.

### Register count (line 124)

- **Not a physical resource by itself:** A program can partition the same qubits into one or many named registers without changing hardware width.
- **Possible intended metric:** Number of logical data/work/ancilla registers or independently addressable hardware banks. These are different notions.
- **Recommendation:** Remove unless a later compiler/API discussion genuinely uses it; otherwise define register partitioning as metadata rather than a cost.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low** in the current unexplained form.

### Simultaneous gate slots (line 124)

- **Potentially useful throughput metric:** Hardware may cap concurrent drives, entanglers, measurements, or operations in a crosstalk group.
- **Not one scalar without gate class:** One-qubit, two-qubit, measurement, transport, and control-channel concurrency differ.
- **Terminology:** “Parallel operation capacity,” “maximum matching under connectivity,” or explicit controller-channel limits may be clearer than “gate slots.”
- **Relation to width:** A device with many qubits can have low exploitable parallelism; this reinforces why width is not “simultaneously acted-on qubits.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High hardware insight** if illustrated.

### Effective qubit reuse rate (line 124)

- **Undefined metric:** Could mean allocation lifetimes per physical qubit, resets per shot/unit time, logical roles per carrier, or fraction of qubits recycled.
- **Quality must accompany rate:** Fast reuse with poor reset fidelity is not beneficial. Include reset latency/error and live-range reduction.
- **Workload dependence:** Reuse is an implementation property, not a fixed vendor performance figure.
- **Recommendation:** Define a precise liveness/recycling statistic or omit the phrase.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Intriguing phrase**, presently foggy.

### Vendor-width reporting claim (line 124, close)

- **Unsupported and doubtful:** Vendors commonly quote physical qubit count; application/benchmark reports quote circuit width, depth, layers, two-qubit-gate count, algorithmic qubits, CLOPS, quantum volume, or error metrics. “Width as the dominant cost” needs named reports.
- **Compilation wording:** Restricted connectivity usually makes routing overhead/depth/two-qubit error central, not width alone. A width that fits may still map poorly.
- **Vendor versus user/compiler:** A submitted circuit’s width is workload metadata; the vendor’s device qubit count is capacity. Do not conflate them.
- **Cross-reference:** §9.12 should explain topology/routing, but it will not substantiate a claim about reporting practices without sources.
- **Better:** “Width is first constrained by available usable qubits; topology then determines whether mapping adds routing operations and depth.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low trust** as written.

### §9.11 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It introduces peak resource reuse and the width–depth design tradeoff at the right moment.
- **Highest-severity defect:** Width is misdefined through simultaneous action, conflating static wire count, peak live qubits, and layer occupancy.
- **Main correctness repair:** Replace categorical NISQ/fault-tolerant winners with feasibility, fidelity, and space-time/Pareto reasoning.
- **Main terminology repair:** Define or remove “qubit-roles,” “register count,” “simultaneous gate slots,” and “effective reuse rate.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.0/10.** The tradeoff is compelling, but unexplained metrics and broad prescriptions reduce confidence.

## Second-pass ledger — `book/part-04-gates-and-circuits/09-quantum-circuits.md` — §9.12 Connectivity Constraints (lines 126–132)

### Heading (line 126)

- **Clear and necessary:** Connectivity is the right next constraint after abstract width/depth.
- **Scope opportunity:** “Connectivity and routing” would better advertise that the section covers both the hardware graph and compiler transformations.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High potential.** Moving quantum data across a machine is naturally visual.

### Coupling-graph definition (line 128, opening)

- **Good first abstraction:** Vertices as physical qubits and edges as permitted pairwise interactions is the standard introductory model.
- **Too binary for real targets:** Edges may be directed, gate-specific, weighted by error/duration, parameter-restricted, disabled by calibration, or available only under scheduling/crosstalk constraints.
- **Multigraph/hypergraph issue:** Different native operations may have different connectivity; native multiqubit/global interactions require hyperedges or richer target descriptions.
- **Time dependence:** Calibration and availability can make the effective graph vary between compilation and execution.
- **“Can be applied” ambiguity:** Distinguish physically possible, currently calibrated, compiler-exposed, and allowed simultaneously.
- **Recommended progression:** Introduce the simple undirected graph, then explicitly label it a lossy abstraction of a hardware target.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High clarity**, with an appealing opportunity for a weighted-map figure.

### Nearly fully connected trapped-ion example (line 128)

- **Directionally correct:** Shared motional modes and shuttling architectures can permit high/all-to-all effective pair connectivity without nearest-neighbor SWAP chains.
- **Overgeneralization:** Not every trapped-ion device exposes every pair with equal fidelity/duration or unlimited simultaneous pair operations; mode crowding, chain length, crosstalk, transport, zones, and calibration matter.
- **Gate wording:** Mølmer–Sørensen interactions may be pairwise addressed or collective/global; “all-to-all Mølmer–Sørensen” risks conflating connectivity with a many-ion global pulse.
- **Architecture distinction:** Static chains and QCCD/shuttling systems achieve effective connectivity differently and incur different movement/scheduling costs.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Physical mechanism would make the contrast memorable.

### Restricted superconducting examples (line 128, close)

- **Broadly correct:** Fixed-frequency/tunable-coupler superconducting processors commonly have sparse planar/local layouts.
- **Examples mix levels:** Heavy-hex and square lattices are topology families; “T-shaped clusters” needs a named architecture/source and may describe a local motif rather than a system-wide family.
- **Currentness/source:** Vendor topology changes quickly; cite named processor generations and access dates if product examples are intended.
- **Sparse does not mean static undirected:** Native CNOT/ECR direction, CZ symmetry, tunable couplers, disabled edges, and calibration quality affect the usable graph.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High visual contrast**, but a topology image would outperform the parenthesis.

### Nonadjacent logical interaction and routing (line 130, opening)

- **Correct default compilation problem:** Under a local two-qubit gate model, the logical states must be brought into an interactable relation or the operation synthesized remotely.
- **“Must be routed” depends on meaning:** Routing can include changing the logical-to-physical mapping, SWAP/move operations, remote-gate decompositions, teleportation, shuttling, or exploiting a native nonlocal primitive. The sentence later lists alternatives, so define routing broadly rather than equating it with SWAP insertion.
- **Logical relabeling:** At circuit boundaries or before measurements, a compiler may update the mapping/classical interpretation without physically swapping states.
- **Direction constraint:** Even adjacent qubits may need basis changes or alternative decompositions when the native interaction is directional.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** “How do distant qubits meet?” is a strong motivating question.

### SWAP-along-a-path explanation (line 130)

- **Correct canonical construction:** Sequential adjacent SWAPs update the placement until operands become neighbors.
- **Mapping nuance:** Usually data need not be swapped back; the compiler can retain the new logical-to-physical assignment and route future gates accordingly.
- **Parallelism:** Disjoint SWAPs can run together, and routing optimizes a global sequence rather than each gate independently.
- **Path choice:** Shortest hop count is not always best if edges differ in error/duration or future interactions favor another placement.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high**, ideal for a before/path/after diagram.

### Alternatives parenthesis (line 130)

- **Valuable breadth:** Bridge/remote-CNOT, physical shuttling, and native long-range interactions prevent the reader from mistaking SWAP networks for universal hardware behavior.
- **Categories overlap:** Shuttling is physical routing; remote-CNOT is gate synthesis/mediated interaction; native long-range coupling eliminates that routing instance. Clarify the taxonomy.
- **Missing alternatives:** Teleportation/entanglement-assisted gates, lattice surgery, moving atoms, photonic switching, bus resonators, and classical output relabeling where applicable.
- **Bridge costs/conditions:** Remote decompositions may preserve logical placement but consume gates/depth/intermediate qubits and propagate noise.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High curiosity**, cramped inside parentheses.

### Three-CNOT SWAP identity (line 130)

- **Correct exact identity:** `SWAP(a,b) = CNOT(a,b) CNOT(b,a) CNOT(a,b)` under the usual ordering convention.
- **Native-direction caveat:** If only one CNOT direction is native, reversing direction may require Hadamards or a different synthesis, though many compilers expose calibrated bidirectional equivalents.
- **Cost dimensions:** It is three CNOT-class entanglers plus possible one-qubit gates; duration/depth/error need not equal three isolated CNOT costs because of scheduling and calibration.
- **Optimization:** A logical SWAP adjacent to other gates can often be absorbed/cancelled/resynthesized more cheaply than compiling it independently.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Excellent concrete fact.** Show the identity rather than only state it.

### “iSWAP/fSim ... implement it for less” (line 130)

- **Unsupported and likely false as a blanket statement:** Native iSWAP/fSim availability does not automatically imply an exact SWAP uses fewer entangling gates than the three-CNOT decomposition. The count depends on the available parameter family, fixed angles, allowed one-qubit rotations, and whether a literal SWAP or only mapping-equivalent behavior is needed.
- **iSWAP is not SWAP:** It adds state-dependent phases; local corrections alone do not make every fixed entangler’s exact synthesis cost obviously “less.”
- **fSim family:** Since fSim parameters vary by hardware and some devices offer SWAP-like interactions, give an explicit decomposition/cost for a named native gate or remove the comparative claim.
- **Compiler co-optimization:** A SWAP plus neighboring logical entangler can sometimes be synthesized as a combined “fermionic SWAP”/SWAP-like block with fewer operations than separate gates; that is a more defensible nuanced point.
- **Severity:** **Material technical suspicion requiring proof.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Interesting claim**, currently invites expert distrust.

### Depth/noise overhead (line 130)

- **Correct directionally:** Additional imperfect operations and longer schedules usually reduce success probability/fidelity.
- **Not monotone per abstract SWAP:** Parallel routing, dynamical decoupling, better calibrated edges, or avoiding a bad direct edge can complicate the relationship.
- **Other overhead:** Mapping can increase one-qubit gates, idle time, crosstalk, calibration exposure, and classical compilation time.
- **Metric:** Estimate added two-qubit layers/error rather than saying generic “noise exposure.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High stakes**, compact and useful.

### Qubit-routing problem definition (line 130)

- **Correct high-level description:** Choose evolving placements and movement operations to realize the interaction sequence at low cost.
- **Objective is plural:** Minimize SWAP count, weighted error, makespan/depth, movement, crosstalk, or some calibrated composite—not one universal “overhead.”
- **Constraints:** Initial/final placement, directed gates, lookahead horizon, ancilla availability, measurement/reset, and parallel moves change the problem.
- **Offline/online distinction:** Compilation can be calibration-aware and may rerun when target properties change.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High algorithmic appeal.**

### NP-hardness claim (line 130)

- **Plausible but needs exact formulation/citation:** Token swapping and various qubit-routing/mapping decision problems are NP-hard/NP-complete, but complexity depends on graph class, gate sequence, parallelism, initial/final mappings, and objective.
- **Do not transfer casually:** “The compiler problem” is a family of problems; cite a theorem for a defined standard formulation.
- **Input-size nuance:** Hardware graph may be fixed in practice while circuit size grows, changing theoretical parameterization.
- **Better:** “Several standard formulations—including minimizing SWAPs for a given interaction sequence—are NP-hard [citation].”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high**, if paired with why greedy heuristics are necessary.

### Heuristic list and production claim (line 130, close)

- **Reasonable families:** Lookahead scoring, search, stochastic/metaheuristic methods, token-swapping approximations, SABRE-like bidirectional passes, and constraint solvers all appear in routing research/tools.
- **A* scaling:** Exact/near-exact A* is often limited to small/local subproblems; saying it is “standard in production compilers” alongside scalable lookahead needs named evidence.
- **Simulated annealing:** Used in mapping research/flows, but “now standard” is a temporal/vendor claim requiring sources.
- **Missing modern methods:** Beam search, dynamic programming on restricted topologies, SAT/SMT/ILP, reinforcement learning, and hybrid partition/local-routing methods—but avoid list inflation unless compared.
- **Name concrete algorithms:** A short SABRE example would be more useful than an ungrounded catalogue.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High**, but the buzzword list needs a result or example.

### Initial-mapping definition (line 132, opening)

- **Correct:** Placement assigns logical qubits to physical qubits before scheduled execution; routing updates that assignment over time.
- **“Complementary” may imply separability:** Initial placement and routing are tightly coupled and often optimized jointly/iteratively.
- **Ancilla/reserved sites:** Mapping may include logical ancillas, empty physical locations, measurement qubits, communication zones, or code patches—not only a bijection of data qubits.
- **Terminology consistency:** Some literature uses “mapping” for the whole placement+routing task and “initial layout” for the starting assignment. Acknowledge this naming variation.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High clarity**, strong compiler analogy.

### Co-location heuristic and “exiles” (line 132)

- **Good intuition:** Frequently/critically interacting qubits should map near one another on high-quality paths.
- **Frequency alone insufficient:** Interaction order, criticality, direction, edge fidelity/duration, readout quality, future routing flexibility, and parallel conflicts matter.
- **“Exiles qubits that do not” is colorful but imprecise:** Noninteracting logical qubits still need good sites/readout and may occupy locations that preserve routing corridors. “Places weakly interacting qubits farther apart” is calmer.
- **Graph formulation:** Weighted logical interaction graph versus weighted physical coupling graph is a useful explicit model.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** “Exiles” is memorable, perhaps overly anthropomorphic but fun.

### Scaling and iterative synthesis-loop claim (line 132, close)

- **Directionally correct:** Joint placement, routing, decomposition, and optimization becomes combinatorial as circuits/devices grow.
- **“Modern compilers” needs examples:** Toolchains differ; name representative passes/documentation rather than universalize.
- **“Run them iteratively” grammar:** Ambiguous antecedent—does “them” mean mapping and routing, circuits, or compilers?
- **Synthesis-loop mechanism:** Decomposition exposes interactions; routing inserts moves; resynthesis cancels/combines gates; updated costs can motivate remapping. Explain this feedback loop explicitly.
- **Very large circuits:** Hierarchical partitioning, modular compilation, windowed routing, and repeated subcircuit structure may be more relevant than simply iterating global synthesis.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High closing idea**, but too vague to visualize.

### §9.12 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** It links physical topology to SWAP overhead and clearly separates initial placement from evolving routing.
- **Highest-severity concern:** The claim that native iSWAP/fSim implements SWAP “for less” is unsupported and gate-parameter dependent; do not publish without an explicit decomposition.
- **Main model repair:** Present coupling graphs as a first abstraction, then add direction, gate type, weights, calibration, concurrency, movement, and hyperedges.
- **Main evidence repair:** Cite exact routing-complexity formulations and named production algorithms rather than declaring a heuristic list standard.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **8.9/10.** Routing is visual, concrete, and consequential; exact examples would make this one of the chapter’s most enjoyable sections.

## Second-pass ledger — `book/part-04-gates-and-circuits/09-quantum-circuits.md` — §9.13 Circuit Optimization (lines 134–146)

### Heading (line 134)

- **Well placed:** Optimization naturally follows metrics and connectivity constraints.
- **Scope:** The section ranges from algebraic circuit rewriting through routing and pulse control; consider “Compilation and circuit optimization” or explicitly bound the abstraction level.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High potential.** Watching redundant gates disappear is intrinsically satisfying.

### Optimization definition (line 136, opening)

- **Strong broad definition:** Search for a semantics-preserving or controlled-approximation implementation with lower target cost.
- **Equivalence must be specified:** Exact unitary equality, equality up to global phase, same action on a subspace, same measured-output distribution, channel/instrument equivalence, or bounded approximation are different contracts.
- **Near-equivalence metric:** Name operator/diamond/trace distance, process infidelity, application-specific observable error, or an explicitly allocated synthesis tolerance.
- **Open/dynamic circuits:** Measurement, reset, noise, classical outputs, and branches require channel/instrument semantics rather than unitary-only equality.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High conceptual trust** if “same behavior” is made testable.

### Cost list (line 136)

- **Useful representative objectives:** Gate count, depth, `$T$` count, and routing overhead cover major layers.
- **Multiobjective conflict:** A rewrite can reduce gate count while increasing depth, lower `$T$` count while using more ancillas, or reduce SWAPs while choosing noisier edges.
- **Missing target-aware costs:** Weighted error, duration, `$T$` depth, qubit count/space-time volume, measurement/reset/feedback latency, crosstalk, control complexity, and expected success probability.
- **“Smaller cost” needs a cost function:** Explain lexicographic objectives, weighted scores, hard constraints, or Pareto fronts.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High**, because tradeoffs prevent optimization from feeling mechanical.

### “Production compilers fall into” taxonomy (line 136, close)

- **Reasonable teaching taxonomy, not exhaustive:** Also commutation analysis, phase-polynomial/ZX-calculus methods, decision-diagram/e-graph rewriting, ancilla management, noise-aware layout, dynamical-decoupling insertion, and verification.
- **Families overlap:** Peephole rewriting can use templates; synthesis can be routing-aware; scheduling and mapping can drive local resynthesis.
- **Temporal claim:** “Production compilers” requires named/versioned examples if the text describes implementation practice rather than general methods.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Good signposting**, but say “common families include.”

### Peephole-rewrite definition (line 138)

- **Correct:** Inspect a bounded local window and replace it with an equivalent lower-cost sequence.
- **Locality may be logical:** Commutation analysis can expose cancellable gates that are not textually adjacent; then it is more than a naïve contiguous peephole.
- **Correctness conditions:** Rewrites must respect parameters, controls, qubit order, barriers/timing, classical dependencies, and target semantics.
- **Noise semantics:** Unitary-equivalent circuits are not necessarily noise-equivalent on hardware.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High accessibility.** Familiar compiler idea transfers well.

### `$HH=I$` example (line 138)

- **Correct exactly:** Hadamard is self-inverse, so consecutive `$H$` gates on the same qubit cancel.
- **Conditions:** They must be consecutive modulo safe commutation and not separated by measurement/reset, an operation on that qubit, or a timing/barrier constraint whose preservation matters.
- **Global phase:** No phase caveat is needed for `$H^2=I$`.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Pleasantly immediate.**

### Adjacent identical-CNOT cancellation (line 138)

- **Correct:** CNOT is self-inverse, so two consecutive applications with the same ordered control and target cancel.
- **“Adjacent” meaning:** They may be separated by gates on disjoint wires and still become cancellable after commutation; gates on control/target require rule-specific checks.
- **Direction matters:** Swapping control and target does not give the same gate.
- **Hardware caveat:** Removing an exact identity is normally beneficial, but scheduled echo/calibration sequences should not be rewritten as abstract CNOTs without preserving physical intent.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High.** Good visual cancellation example.

### Rotation merging (line 138)

- **Correct for same-axis rotations on the same qubit:** `$R_Z(\alpha)R_Z(\beta)=R_Z(\alpha+\beta)$` under the chapter’s convention, since the generators commute.
- **Ordering harmless here:** Both factors commute, but retain a consistent circuit-composition convention.
- **Modulo/global phase:** Normalize angles according to the gate convention/target; some gate families differ by global phase under periodic reduction.
- **Symbolic parameters:** Merging may simplify or complicate parameterized-circuit execution and gradient structure; compilers may preserve parameters intentionally.
- **Across controls:** Controlled rotations or conditional operations do not merge under the same simple rule without matching controls/branches.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** Readers see algebra become compilation.

### Cheap/repeated-until-quiescent claim (line 138, close)

- **Broadly plausible for local passes:** Pattern lookup/local algebra is usually inexpensive relative to global routing or synthesis.
- **Termination not automatic:** Rewrite systems need an oriented decreasing measure or cycle prevention; independently “simplifying” rules can oscillate.
- **Quiescence criterion:** Production pipelines may stop when size/depth is unchanged, on a fixed iteration count, or on pass-manager conditions—not necessarily a formal normal form.
- **Local minimum:** Quiescence under one rule set does not imply global optimality; an temporarily cost-increasing rewrite can enable a larger later reduction.
- **Current concrete example:** Qiskit documents low-level optimization loops until circuit size/depth stabilize at some optimization levels, but exact pass sets vary by version/level.
- **Source checked 22 July 2026:** [Qiskit transpiler overview and optimization stages](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit/1.3/transpiler).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High compiler insight**, with a fun “rewrite loop” pitfall available.

### Template-matching definition (line 140)

- **Correct broad idea:** Match a subcircuit against one side of a known identity and substitute a cheaper equivalent.
- **Overlap with peepholes:** Templates are a mechanism for local/mid-scale rewrites; explain distinction by window size, parameterization, or identity-library search.
- **Match complexity:** Qubit permutations, symbolic parameters, commutation, and embedding a template in a larger DAG complicate matching.
- **Cost orientation:** An identity has no intrinsically “simpler” side across every target; choose using the current hardware cost model.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Moderate-to-high**, more engaging with one nontrivial before/after template.

### Compiler “database” claim (line 140)

- **Overliteral:** Equivalences may be hard-coded as rewrite rules, generated algebraically, stored in an equivalence library, implemented by specialized passes, or discovered through synthesis—not necessarily a database.
- **Toffoli identities vague:** Name one decomposition/rewrite and its cost assumptions. Relative-phase Toffoli replacements are not generally equivalent unless surrounding computation permits the phases.
- **Chapter/appendix identities:** A textbook identity is not automatically a safe compiler template when gate direction, global/relative phase, controls, noise, or timing constraints differ.
- **Recommended:** “Compilers encode equivalences in rule libraries and specialized passes.”
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Low in abstract form**; a concrete template would fix this.

### Synthesis-based optimization definition (line 142)

- **Correct and important:** Collect a block, characterize its semantics, and synthesize a cheaper implementation for the target.
- **Replacement guard:** Compare the synthesized result under the chosen metric and retain it only when semantics/tolerance and cost improve.
- **Block choice:** Maximal one-/two-qubit runs, Clifford blocks, linear reversible functions, phase polynomials, or connected hardware subgraphs have specialized synthesis methods.
- **Verification:** Numerical equality/tolerance or formal equivalence checking is especially important for generated replacements.
- **Current concrete example:** IBM documents block collection and re-synthesis passes that replace only if a cost such as CNOT count improves; that is a stronger example than a generic claim.
- **Source checked 22 July 2026:** [IBM circuit synthesis passes](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/ai-transpiler-passes).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high.** “Throw away the implementation and rediscover it” is a compelling idea.

### KAK example (line 142)

- **Appropriate for two-qubit unitary synthesis:** Cartan/KAK decomposition characterizes a two-qubit unitary up to local one-qubit operations and supports target-entangler minimization.
- **Scope:** It is not a generic small-block algorithm for arbitrary qubit count, measurements, or dynamic control.
- **Hardware awareness:** Exact entangler count depends on the native two-qubit gate family and permitted local gates.
- **Cross-reference:** §8.14 should use the same convention/canonical region and explain how it becomes an optimizer.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High payoff** for earlier mathematics.

### Solovay–Kitaev example (line 142)

- **Misleading as a production optimization example:** Solovay–Kitaev proves efficient approximation over suitable finite universal gate sets, but modern fault-tolerant single-qubit synthesis generally uses more specialized/efficient number-theoretic or search methods.
- **Purpose mismatch:** It synthesizes an approximation to a target unitary; it does not inherently optimize an existing block better than pattern matching.
- **Cost scaling:** Its polylogarithmic asymptotic exponent and large constants make it pedagogically foundational but often practically inferior.
- **Better:** Present it as a theoretical synthesis guarantee, then name practical Clifford+`$T$` methods or avoid production implications.
- **Severity:** **Material taxonomy/current-practice concern.**
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Good callback**, but experts will question the tool choice.

### Numerical pulse-level optimization example (line 142)

- **Layer conflation:** Pulse optimal control searches analog control waveforms under a Hamiltonian/device model; it is not simply circuit-block re-synthesis in a discrete gate IR.
- **Cross-layer compilation is real:** A circuit block can be lowered directly to a pulse, potentially outperforming gate-by-gate decomposition, but equivalence/fidelity and calibration are physical-model dependent.
- **Access caveat:** Some vendors no longer expose user pulse-level control even though internal calibration/optimal-control techniques remain.
- **Terminology:** Separate **unitary/gate synthesis** from **pulse-level optimal control** as adjacent families.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high futuristic appeal**, needs its own sentence.

### Expense and ability to escape pattern limits (line 142, close)

- **Correct:** Search/resynthesis usually costs more compilation time but can cross local rewrite barriers.
- **Not guaranteed shorter:** It may fail, return a worse circuit, trade one metric for another, or introduce approximation error; production passes often use replacement thresholds.
- **Caching:** Frequently synthesized blocks can be cached/precomputed, changing compile-time cost.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High and credible** with a “keep only if better” rule.

### Routing-aware reordering (line 144)

- **Important co-optimization:** Gate ordering, commutation, scheduling, placement, routing, and decomposition interact.
- **Too narrow as a family:** Routing-aware synthesis can change gate decompositions or logical ordering, not merely interleave scheduling and SWAP insertion.
- **Semantic condition:** Only independent or commuting operations can be reordered freely; dynamic/classical dependencies constrain motion.
- **Objective:** “Total cost” again needs definition—SWAP count, two-qubit error, makespan, fidelity, or calibrated score.
- **Relation to §9.12:** This could be merged into that section or expanded with a before/after example here.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High practical value**, currently only a label.

### “You do not write these passes” advice (line 146)

- **Good beginner reassurance:** Most users should start with maintained compiler pipelines rather than hand-implement optimizers.
- **Too absolute:** Researchers, compiler developers, and advanced users do write/customize pass managers and plugins; even application developers may need domain-specific rewrites.
- **Better:** “Most users begin by calling a compiler and selecting/configuring a pipeline.”
- **Validation obligation:** Users should still test semantic equivalence, inspect mappings, set seeds, and benchmark output rather than trust an optimization level blindly.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Friendly and practical**, slightly dismissive of advanced readers.

### Tool terminology parenthesis (line 146)

- **Qiskit is current:** “Transpile” is established Qiskit terminology; current docs expose staged pass managers and optimization levels 0–3.
- **tket typography/command needs verification:** `$\mathrm{t}|\mathrm{ket}\rangle$` is branding, not necessarily the exact user-facing method verb/API. Cite current pytket documentation and consider writing “pytket compilation passes.”
- **Cirq claim needs verification:** Cirq uses transformer/optimization APIs whose names and recommended entry points evolve; “optimize” may be a concept rather than one universal call.
- **Framework asymmetry:** Qiskit’s `transpile`, a generic “compile,” and generic “optimize” are not equivalent API granularity. Give versioned code snippets or keep the advice framework-neutral.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **High utility**, vulnerable to API aging.

### Optimization-level advice (line 146)

- **Correct for Qiskit-like preset pipelines:** Effort levels provide a convenient tradeoff between compile time and expected output quality.
- **Not monotonic quality:** Current Qiskit documentation explicitly warns level 3 is not guaranteed to produce the best result; passes may be stochastic.
- **Reproducibility:** Set compiler seeds where supported and compare several runs/levels on the actual target/cost metric.
- **Approximation:** Some knobs may permit near-equivalent transformations; users must understand the tolerance contract.
- **Source checked 22 July 2026:** [Qiskit transpiler optimization behavior](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit/1.3/transpiler); [Qiskit optimization-level guide](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/set-optimization).
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Very high actionable advice** after these caveats.

### Debugging “blow-ups” and Chapter 23 forward reference (line 146, close)

- **Excellent motivation:** Compilation can add routing gates, decompose high-level operations, allocate ancillas, or expand precision-sensitive synthesis; knowing stages helps locate the source.
- **Define blow-up:** Track width, depth, two-qubit count, duration, `$T$` resources, and mapping changes before/after each stage.
- **Debug method:** Seed the compiler, inspect staged IR/callback metrics, lock layout/routing methods, and compare target-free versus target-aware passes.
- **Forward-reference burden:** Chapter 23 is distant; include a minimal diagnostic checklist now.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **Exceptional practical close.** Readers recognize a real frustration and gain agency.

### §9.13 local synthesis

- **Strongest feature:** The section offers a compact mental map from algebraic cancellation through block resynthesis to routing co-optimization.
- **Highest-severity concerns:** “Near-equivalent” lacks a metric; Solovay–Kitaev is misleading as a production optimization example; pulse optimization is mixed into the circuit-synthesis layer.
- **Main current-practice repair:** Use named/versioned compiler pipelines, explain stochastic/nonmonotonic optimization levels, and avoid assuming all frameworks expose equivalent verbs.
- **Main pedagogical repair:** Show one before/after example for each family and state its semantic contract/cost metric.
- **Reader entertainment/engagement:** **9.1/10.** Gate cancellation and resynthesis are highly satisfying; concrete transformations would make the section sing.
